“I read your message at two fourteen,” I say. “I typed *Great*. Then I deleted it. I typed *How long?* and deleted that too. By dinner I knew I was hoping you'd get scared when I didn't answer. I wanted you to come back and ask what you'd done to me.”

Paloma picks a loose thread from her shorts. “I checked the chat at every gas stop for two weeks.”

“Why didn't you send another message?” The defense escapes before I recognize it.

“I sent the first one.”

“You did.”

“And you saw it.”

“Yes.” I press my palms against my knees. “It wasn't space. I was punishing you because I couldn't stop you from going.”

She looks beyond me into the empty rooms. Wind moves through them now, tapping something metal at uneven intervals.

“I'm going Saturday,” she says. “I want the job. I want the cabin and the boots and mornings where nobody has known us since second grade. I waited until the papers were signed to tell you because I didn't want to be talked out of it. That's mine to answer for. It doesn't make the nine weeks mine.”

“No.”

“I would have gone if you'd asked me to stay.”

“I know.”

“You didn't know. You kept checking.”

The needle descends another fraction.

“I'm sorry,” I say.

Paloma winds the loose thread once around her finger. “I remember you saying that already.”

She reaches for the flashlight. “Below half, then water. Hold this while I pour.”

We wait with both doors open. The extra stars fade without pattern, leaving the ordinary ones separated by dark. No sound marks the change. The motor court remains: blue doors, tiled fish, the lane Paloma found behind the last room. At 12:19 the temperature needle drops below half.

Paloma wraps her overshirt around her hand, loosens the reservoir cap a little at a time, and waits through the last release of pressure. I hold the light while she pours in one bottle. The whole bottle brings the level to the lower mark. The second stays unopened between our seats.

The engine starts on the third try. The belt's squeal is rougher than before, but the temperature holds below three-quarters. Paloma backs away from the pool, turns between the office and the last room, and finds the service lane.

It is one strip of cracked pavement with sand banked along both sides. The radio catches a woman announcing livestock notices, loses her, then settles into ordinary static. We pass no station, motor court, or fork. The dark ahead stays dark until the sky begins to gray.

Forty minutes later, the lane meets a divided highway. Its paint is fresh enough to shine. A green sign promises fuel in nine miles without naming a town. The paper itinerary has slipped under my seat; by its distances, the odometer contains thirty-one miles that do not belong anywhere.

Paloma keeps the wheel. My job is to hold the flashlight on the temperature gauge whenever the dash light blinks out. A pale band of morning gathers above the road.

After several miles, Paloma says, “After my first week.”

I look over.

“One text,” she says. “Not before. If I answer, ask whether I can call. If I don't answer, leave it.”

Questions crowd up: what time, what if the crew has no signal, how long *leave it* means. I say none of them.

“All right,” I say.

“I might still say no.”

The dash goes dark. Paloma taps the clear plastic over the gauges once, then points. “Light.”

I move the beam back to the temperature needle.

stories.title: The Players Above
stories.prompt: "I apreciate your advice, formless voice, but what do you want with me?" "Me and some friends are having a cosmic game. One of us has created a great peril and the rest of us must guide you and your companions to both figure it out and then solve it" "Like in a TTRPG?" "Oh, you have those too?"
stories.body:
# The Players Above

Anjali Bose had been ignoring the voice for six minutes when it ruined a perfectly good trap.

On Malik's battle map, her brass scout stood before a moss-painted arch. Devika's wounded knight waited three squares behind, one paper hit point from collapse. Anjali intended to cross the pressure plate, spring the ceiling blade, and leave the passage safe for both of them. Malik watched from behind his game screen with the stillness of a man who had designed exactly this mistake.

*The left stone is false,* the voice told her. *Move around it.*

It had been right about the wasp under her coffee lid on Tuesday. It had been right about the loose wheel on a grocery cart and the stranger who would step backward off a bus without looking. Each warning arrived inside her thoughts, clear and patient, then refused every question about its source.

Anjali lifted her miniature off the map instead of moving it.

“I appreciate your advice, formless voice, but what do you want with me?”

Malik lowered his screen. Devika's knight stayed pinched between two fingers.

The answer carried a sudden, delighted warmth. *Me and some friends are having a cosmic game. One of us has created a great peril, and the rest of us must guide you and your companions to both figure it out and then solve it.*

Anjali looked at the painted dungeon, the rain shaking the cabin windows, and the steel case of dice between the snack bowls. “Like in a TTRPG?”

*Oh, you have those too?*

Every die in the open case rose onto one edge.

The four-sided die balanced on a point. Across the room, a teaspoon stood upright in Malik's coffee. The effect spread to the woodstove, where three flakes of ash met tip to tip above the coals and hung there without falling.

Something struck the north wall hard enough to jump the framed photograph over the mantel.

Malik was under the table before Anjali moved. “Down. Mine says it sees through glass.”

Devika dropped beside him. “Since when do you have a mine?”

“Eleven days. Yours says the back door, doesn't it?”

Devika did not answer. The window over the sink lost its reflection. A strip of blackness crossed it from sill to frame, bent in the middle, and bent again where nothing with a joint should have. Rain touched it and disappeared.

Anjali crawled away from the window. “That had better not be the peril.”

*It is called the Countermove by the one who placed it. We expected it to begin farther from you.*

“You misplaced a monster?”

*No. Its anchor was placed correctly. You were not expected to gather so soon.*

Another blow bowed the kitchen door inward. Malik reached up and killed the lamps. Firelight flattened them against the floor while a narrow point scratched from one window to the next, tasting the cabin's edges.

“What does it do?” Anjali asked.

*It occupies the route its opponents are most likely to take. Each correct interception gives it more reach. If it reaches the road after dawn, it will have hundreds of routes to learn instead of three.*

Malik's parents used the cabin road before breakfast. So did the bakery van, the marina crew, and anyone driving east around the lake. In rain, the first gray light could be less than two hours away.

“Can it follow us over water?”

*Not efficiently. Your strongest move is the dock.*

A single route arranged the night into something Anjali could do.

Malik shook his head before she spoke. “Mine says there is something solid inside it. That's all it will commit to.”

“Solid can drown,” Anjali said. “We take the boat.”

Devika had already pulled the car keys from their hook. She pocketed them, then took the iron poker from beside the stove. “I am coming with whoever opens a door first.”

It was not agreement, but the north wall groaned again. Malik gave them each a rain jacket and led them through the mudroom on hands and knees. The voice warned Anjali to keep left. She repeated the instruction. Nobody asked why it knew.

They burst outside together.

Cold rain needled Anjali's face. The dock lay below them, past twenty wooden steps and a narrow beach. Malik's flashlight cut a white bar through the spruce. For the first ten steps there was only wet bark, silver gravel, and the boat bumping softly against its fenders.

At the eleventh, Devika stopped so abruptly Anjali struck her back.

The darkness beneath the trees had acquired corners.

It unfolded across the stairway in long connected spars. One planted itself on the dock. Another hooked the handrail. Three more met above the path and flexed downward, a cage assembling around the place where the voice had told Anjali to stand.

Malik swung the flashlight low. Its beam passed under the nearest spar and found a black polyhedron turning at the center of the shape. It was the size of a grapefruit and all edge, each face swallowing light without reflection.

“Solid,” he said. “There.”

The thing struck.

Devika shoved Anjali off the step. A point punched through two stair boards where Anjali's knee had been. Malik fell against the rail, and a second spar pinned his jacket to the wood. Devika brought the poker down on it. Iron rang; the black length did not break, but it loosened enough for Malik to tear free.

“Cabin,” he said.

“It has the cabin.” Anjali could see another limb dragging itself uphill between the trees.

“The cabin has doors. Move.”

They climbed as the Countermove gathered behind them. The path lights went dark one by one, not extinguished but covered. At the top, Anjali turned and saw the polyhedron pull its limbs after it. The whole creature had been built around that one hard piece.

Devika yanked the mudroom door open. A black point swept over their heads as they dove through. Malik kicked the door shut, dropped the oak bench against it, and wedged a split log beneath the handle. Something hit the outside. The bench skidded the width of Anjali's palm.

“Screws,” Malik said. “Red toolbox under the porch worktable.”

Devika had the door open before either of them caught her. She slipped through the gap, leaving the car keys on the floor, and vanished into the rain.

“Devika!”

The Countermove was dragging itself toward the lake. One limb passed above the steps. Another searched the beach. None turned toward the small figure crouching beside the porch.

Devika snatched the red toolbox from beneath the outdoor worktable and came back at a run. Malik pulled her inside by the back of her jacket. The door slammed. A black point struck the porch a full second too late.

“You heard me,” Malik said.

“I heard you. Mine didn't.” She pushed the toolbox against his chest. “I moved before it could improve the idea.”

Anjali grabbed the keys from the floor. “Did your voice send you?”

Devika wiped rain out of her eyes. “Mine was busy telling me to run north without you.”

Malik opened the toolbox. “How long?”

“Since the thing touched the dock.” Devika tore a packet of deck screws open with her teeth. “It says two deaths are better than three. I disagree with its arithmetic.”

The bench jumped again. Malik drove the first screw through its leg and into the floor. “Hold that end.”

Anjali held it while he worked, though every instinct in her wanted the map, the facts, the one missing inference. “Mine says it wants all of us alive.”

“Yours likes you,” Devika said. “That is not the same guarantee.”

*The road is briefly open,* the voice said. *Take the car now. If the others remain, the Countermove may follow you away from them.*

The car alarm began to scream uphill.

All three of them looked toward the road-facing window. A branching shadow covered the glass. Metal crumpled outside; the alarm cut off mid-wail.

Malik stopped turning the screwdriver. “Mine said the car would be hit before yours did, but the thing was still below us. Then your voice named the road.”

“You can't know which came first.”

“I can know where the dents are.” He pointed the screwdriver toward the ceiling. “Mine says the roof beams will hold longer than the doors. If it tells me the loft is safest, watch what happens.”

“Don't feed it another—”

His gaze went distant for half a breath. Above them, claws of blackness raked across the shingles.

Malik nodded once. “That's enough.”

Anjali's voice pressed close. *The car remains your best chance. You are quicker at choosing than the others. Go before they make the choice for you.*

She closed her fist around the keys. The road would draw the creature from the cabin. If she could reach the car, if Malik's guide was wrong, if speed counted for more than trust—

Devika held out her hand. “Keys.”

“I can pull it uphill.”

“Keys.”

“It follows the likeliest route. Give it one.”

Devika stepped close enough that Anjali could smell rain and iron on her jacket. “Mine told me the same plan with your name where mine is. I didn't call that rescue.”

Malik set down the screwdriver. “The roof when my voice named the loft. The car when hers named the road. The steps when yours named the dock. Motive can wait.”

The keys bit Anjali's palm. Her voice had saved her from small disasters for weeks. Tonight every clean instruction had become another joint in the thing outside.

She gave the keys to Devika.

“You said we had to figure it out and solve it,” Anjali told the voice. “What did you leave out?”

*We did not leave out—*

“What ends it?”

The presence withdrew, as if consulting a rulebook she could not see. The Countermove hammered the cabin again. One deck screw pulled half out of the floor.

*The anchor must be separated from its reaching body. Then one of us can open the placement path and take it back. We cannot touch it while the body encloses it.*

“Does it hear us?”

*No.*

“Thoughts?”

*No. It receives the forecasts registered by the players. Strong agreement gives it a narrow body. Uncertainty forces it to divide its reach.*

Malik measured the steel dice case between his hands. “Your advice is rangefinding.”

*Our advice has prevented three deaths.*

“And Devika crossed the porch when none of you called the move,” Anjali said. “From now until I ask for the path, you say nothing.”

*A guide cannot abandon a chosen—*

“Then lose.”

The voice went still.

Devika spoke aloud to someone Anjali could not hear. Her side of the exchange lasted four words: “No. Watch me leave.” Malik listened longer, jaw working, before he said, “Measurements after. Not during.”

With the voices gone, Anjali could hear the deck screws ticking loose in the floor. Outside, the Countermove scraped from the crushed car to the roof and back toward the dock, stretched among three stale answers.

Malik turned over the battle map. On its blank side he drew the cabin and the old fire ring north of it. “The solid part was uphill of the dock when we saw it. It has to move through the clearing to reach all three sides.”

“We find it with these.” Anjali plucked the balanced four-sided die from the case.

She set it on the floor. It fell onto a face. At the north wall, the same die rocked once and rose onto a point.

Malik tested three more. Near the kitchen they rolled normally. Beside the cold fireplace, a twelve-sided die stopped on an edge despite the slanting hearthstone. Near the anchor, balance had too many answers. A pine needle outside could bridge between two wet stones. A dropped washer rested upright in mud.

They followed those small impossibilities along the walls while the creature worried at the cabin. The strongest distortion pointed toward the old fire ring.

Their tools were what the cabin offered. Devika bent the poker's hooked end wider and tied it to the orange boat line. Malik emptied his dice into a cooking pot and worked the damaged clasp of the steel case until it shut without sticking. Anjali found three lanterns, only one bright enough to show the anchor through the black body.

She began assigning routes. Devika cut her off.

“No. You pick people too fast.”

“Somebody has to carry each thing.”

“The die picks who. We decide what.”

Malik put the twelve-sided die beneath an enamel mug. Four numbers for each rotation: hook on the ridge, hook in the wash, hook by the lake. The box and bright lantern would rotate with it. Every person rehearsed every tool once, badly and in silence. Anjali's first throw with the line tangled around her boot. Malik could not swing it without telegraphing his shoulder. Devika snapped the dice case shut so hard the clasp jammed.

They corrected the failures, then carried all three sets of supplies to the fork below the fire ring. No one chose a path. No one asked above.

The Countermove had become a black web among the trees. A limb lay across the ridge. Two probed the wash. Another hovered over the lakeside trail. Unable to settle on one expected arrangement, it had spent itself covering all of them. At its center, the anchor flickered between gaps.

Malik crouched over the mug. “Once I lift, don't repeat the number.”

“Don't explain it either,” Devika said. “Move your feet.”

He shook the mug against a flat stone. The die knocked twelve possible answers around inside the dark.

When Malik lifted the mug, the upper face showed eleven.

Devika seized the hooked line and ran up the ridge. Malik took the case into the wash. Anjali caught the bright lantern and sprinted along the lakeward path.

The Countermove chose late.

Its ridge limb stabbed where Malik would have been in the first arrangement. The wash closed around an absent hook. By the time the lakeside branch found Anjali, she had already thrown herself under it. Cold blackness passed over her back without weight or texture, erasing the patter of rain for one breath.

She came up inside the fire ring and raised the lantern.

The Countermove folded toward the light. That move, at least, it could predict from her body. Its nearest spars gathered above her while the others tore free of the wrong routes. Between them the anchor hung naked, revolving in a nest of hair-thin black cords.

Malik slid down the wash on one knee and shoved the open dice case beneath it.

Devika's first cast of the poker passed high. She hauled the line back hand over hand. The creature bent toward her. A pointed limb punched into the ridge and trapped the loose cord.

“Leave it,” Anjali shouted.

Devika looked at the pinned line, then at the anchor. She did not obey. She ran downhill, straight at the limb, and kicked the cord free an instant before the black point struck again. Her second cast caught one sharp corner of the polyhedron.

Malik braced the case with both hands. “Now.”

Devika pulled. The black cords tightened. Anjali swung the lantern into them. Its wire cage crumpled against something with no visible surface. Glass burst, and the cords sprang apart under the blow long enough for the anchor to tear loose.

It dropped into the case.

Malik slammed the lid. The Countermove collapsed toward him, every spar reversing at once. One wrapped his forearm; another hooked his boot and dragged him through the fire ring. He kept both hands on the box.

Anjali reached for the silence inside her mind. “Path. Under Malik.”

The voice answered without commentary. *Opened.*

A gray seam divided the mud beneath Malik's shoulder. It widened into depth without revealing any place beyond. Malik rolled, dragging the case across it. The steel corner vanished. The black limbs pulled harder, stripping stones from the fire ring and bending the nearest sapling nearly flat.

Devika dropped the poker and grabbed Malik's jacket. Anjali threw her weight against the back of the case. For one second the clasp hung at the seam, half here and half nowhere.

Then it passed through.

The Countermove followed its anchor. Spars ripped out of the trees and poured into the gray opening, narrowing as they went. The limb around Malik's arm vanished last. The seam closed on empty mud.

Rain reached the ground again.

Malik stayed on his back, feeling along his forearm. The sleeve was torn, but the skin beneath showed only a dark bruise. Devika sat in the wet ashes with the orange line looped around both wrists. Anjali waited for the voice to name the victory.

It kept silent.

“Good,” she said, and helped Malik stand.

By dawn, the cabin had a cracked window, a ruined porch step, and one door that still latched. Malik taped plastic over the glass while Devika returned the car keys to their hook. She did not offer an explanation, and Anjali did not ask for one. They made coffee in a saucepan while the abandoned teaspoon lay at the bottom of a cold cup.

Malik put the twelve-sided die at the center of the table. “This one is not going into evidence.”

“You don't have evidence,” Devika said. “You mailed it through a hole in the ground.”

“I have an invoice for a windshield.”

Anjali's laugh came out once, sharp and unfinished. Her hands had begun shaking now that nothing needed them. She set her brass scout beside the die.

The voice waited until she addressed it.

“Now you may speak.”

*Our peril is contained. The others ask whether your table will continue the game.*

“No.”

Its surprise was colder than its delight had been. *Never?*

“You don't get that answer yet.” Anjali turned the enamel mug upside down over the die. “If there is another game, we make the danger. You answer when one of us calls. Nothing is placed here unless all three of us lift this cup.”

Devika put both hands in her lap. Malik resumed winding tape around the broken window frame.

*The one who made the Countermove will object.*

“Then it can play without pieces.”

The voice receded. For a long moment there was only tape tearing, coffee beginning to boil, and rainwater ticking from their jackets onto the floor.

When it returned, it spoke without warmth. *No piece will be placed until your cup rises.*

Anjali looked at her friends. No one reached for the mug.

“Then wait.”

stories.title: A Very Good Dog
stories.prompt: The ultimate evil guy turns themselves into the pet (Dog) of the hero to break into their home and do bad things but then being a pet is dope, they just chill and no one knows where he went.
stories.body:
# A Very Good Dog

At exactly ten on Tuesday morning, Brightguard’s pampered dog stole the butler’s shoe with Maledict’s human mouth.

Pickle was alive, unharmed, and enthusiastically dog-minded inside the adult body of the most feared villain in the Tri-City Area. He had dropped to all fours the instant the paired circles stopped flashing. Now he bounded across the top laboratory of Maledict’s glass-and-steel skyscraper, a polished black shoe clenched between his teeth, while the butler pursued him past enough weapon controls to spoil several districts.

On the other circle, Maledict occupied Pickle’s living body: rough brown coat, heavy tail, and one forepaw white with natural fur from the ankle down. He watched his own human knees skid under a console and told himself this indignity had a precise end.

“Fourteen hours, sir.” The butler caught Pickle around the waist before Maledict’s body could shoulder a cabinet marked for catastrophic use. “At midnight, I keep your body inside the west circle. You bite the plate inside the collar for five seconds. Both signals engage, or neither mind moves.”

Maledict knew this. He had designed the return to require both occupied bodies and his local trigger, because no subordinate would ever be able to recall him by force. He had never imagined himself becoming the uncooperative half. He tried to order the butler to stop reciting instructions.

His borrowed throat produced a bark. Maledict’s tail struck the silver floor twice.

“I will record that as confirmation.”

The butler reclaimed one wet shoe. Pickle immediately seized the other.

A pet shuttle waited in the private loading bay below. Brightguard expected Pickle back from his regular grooming appointment at ten thirty; Maledict had diverted the automated shuttle to the tower, where the butler guided the dog onto the circle, and its route would now resume. Pickle’s face, collar, scent, and white forepaw would carry poison and a lock override through every security layer in Brightguard’s home. At midnight, Maledict would return to his own body with Brightguard dead and the live code from her counterseal transmitted to his skyscraper.

The butler opened the shuttle cage. Maledict stepped in.

Behind him, Pickle climbed into Maledict’s throne, turned three circles on the leather, and sat on the villain’s cape.

Fourteen hours.

The shuttle reached Brightguard’s townhouse at ten thirty-two. The gate read Pickle’s collar, the front step read his paws, and the door unlocked for an animal who had lived there for six years. Maledict walked into warm timber, pale concrete, and the faint electronic hum of a modern hero’s home.

A rescue drone charged above the coat rack. Flexible armor hung beside a rain jacket. On the wall, a city display tracked bridge loads, hospital capacity, and storm runoff across all three municipalities of the Tri-City Area.

Brightguard came from the kitchen wearing charcoal training clothes under the open upper half of a silver rescue suit. Her hair had gone mostly gray, cropped close around the ports behind her ears. Fine lines bracketed her eyes; an old impact brace wrapped one knee. She had spent thirty years hauling people out of wreckage and still moved as if every room might tilt.

“There you are.” She touched two fingers to the dark screen on her wrist. “Badge.”

Maledict sat.

“That’s not badge.”

He had studied her patrol roster, alarm latency, drone maintenance, utility tunnels, and the molecular tolerances of her armor. No report had mentioned badge.

Brightguard held her palm low. “White paw.”

Pickle’s shoulder moved before Maledict ordered it. The naturally white forepaw slapped her hand. At once the dog body twisted toward a red rubber ball in the entry basket. Motor memory, then: movement without memory, a trace in muscles that knew nothing of Maledict’s plans.

Brightguard nudged the ball toward him. “Now steal it.”

Maledict picked it up and placed it neatly at her feet.

She stared. “You never surrender the red one.”

He snatched it back.

“You make me chase you.”

She reached. Maledict dodged under the bench, pivoted around the stair rail, and crossed the kitchen with Brightguard behind him. Pickle’s legs supplied the balance; Maledict supplied an escape route calculated from three reflected surfaces. He ended behind the dining table with the ball pinned between both paws.

Brightguard stopped on the other side, breathing harder than she would have ten years ago and smiling despite it. “That’s closer.”

The remark was data. Maledict filed it with the palm, the white paw, and the compulsory theft. Intimate habits were only another security system, though an unusually frivolous one.

Brightguard opened a cabinet painted with Pickle’s pawprint. Rows of transparent bins occupied three shelves: salmon coins, liver knots, dried pumpkin, dental braids, emergency cheese, and something labeled QUIET TUESDAY. A refrigerator drawer beneath held portions dated by day.

She selected a salmon coin. “Grooming tax.”

Its smell reached him before her hand did. Maledict recoiled.

Brightguard lowered the treat. “You love salmon.”

He turned toward her lunch board instead. On it lay sliced cucumber, precise and green. Cucumber appeared at diplomatic tables. Cucumber had standards. He stole a piece.

“You bury cucumber under my workbench.”

He chewed without breaking eye contact. The dog tongue found it cool and bitter but tolerable.

Brightguard crouched. Humor left her face with professional speed. “Eyes.”

He backed away.

“Pickle. Eyes.”

She lifted each eyelid, checked his gums, then ran practiced fingers along his jaw and neck. The health panel on her wrist woke. A shallow scan passed harmlessly over him; a deeper one would reach the shielded compartments in his collar.

“Salmon,” she said, holding the coin close. “If you refuse it twice, we call the clinic.”

Maledict took it to prevent the scan.

Fat and salt burst across his tongue. His back legs folded without permission. He sat, swallowed, and looked at the cabinet.

Brightguard watched his ears. “There you are. Chew the next one.”

He chewed the next one. Slowly. For operational reasons.

At the skyscraper, the butler replaced Maledict’s second shoe with a length of braided climbing rope. Pickle abandoned the shoe and charged away with the rope, towing one end around a marble column.

“An acceptable exchange,” the butler said. “Please avoid the red doors.”

Pickle ran straight for the red doors.

The butler used the tower controls to lock them, then muted a call from Maledict’s senior staff. It returned at once. Pickle sprang toward the moving faces on the wall display and planted both human hands on it.

For half a second, Maledict’s motor habits straightened the spine and arranged the right hand into his familiar gesture of command. The six callers fell silent. Then Pickle saw the butler raise the rope and lunged out of frame, grinning with all of Maledict’s teeth.

The butler stepped before the camera. “The master will not appear in full.”

A voice from the display asked whether the morning’s citywide threat would proceed.

“No. Recall the drones and hold all field teams inside the tower.”

“We have no authentication.”

Behind the butler, Pickle found a touch panel. One cheerful slap began opening the armored roof.

The butler killed power to the panel. “You now have a direct order. Execute it before his patience changes.”

He ended the call, closed the roof, and removed a decorative obsidian rod from Pickle’s mouth.

“That controls orbital targeting, sir. The rope is yours.”

Pickle took the rope and knocked over the throne.

By noon, Maledict had mapped Brightguard’s ground floor and acquired four salmon coins.

A news pane floated over the kitchen counter. His face occupied half of it beneath a red banner: MALEDICT MISSING AFTER ENERGY SURGE. Transit officers searched service tunnels under the eastern municipality. Brightguard’s colleagues were checking known bunkers. The public had been told to report any unusual drone activity and not to approach his skyscraper.

Maledict lay beneath the counter, unrecognized, and approved of the scale of the confusion.

Brightguard swiped the pane aside. “Middle.”

He moved to her left knee, the disciplined heel position used by his own guard animals.

She tapped both thighs. “Between, Pickle. You only heel near traffic.”

The scanner on her wrist was still awake. Pickle’s legs chose before Maledict could object, walking between hers and turning so his shoulders rested against her shins.

“Good.” Her hand checked the base of his ears again, searching for heat or swelling. “If you wobble, stop eating, or forget who I am, we go in. One weird morning I can watch.”

Maledict leaned just enough to keep her from restarting the scan.

A rescue alert chimed. Brightguard crossed to the equipment wall, and Maledict followed because the reinforced compartment containing her counterseal lay upstairs beyond the washroom. When she entered that washroom to seal the ports of her suit, he slipped in behind her and stepped directly into the dry shower for a better view through the bedroom door.

Brightguard paused with one gauntlet half fastened. “You heard me think the word bath last week and hid in the recycling cupboard.”

Maledict stepped out.

“No. You volunteered.” She touched the shower control. “Medic rinse while I suit up.”

He backed toward the door.

“Too late.”

Warm water descended. The floor heated under his paws. Adjustable jets worked shampoo through his coat while Brightguard, now armored to the waist, scrubbed the difficult patch beneath his collar. Maledict had endured volcanic restraints with fewer amenities. A rubber mat prevented slips. Towels waited in a warming drawer. The rinse ended with a low stream behind his ears that made one rear leg begin thumping.

Brightguard caught the leg gently. “That part hasn’t changed.”

She dried him, checked the collar without finding its hidden cavities, then left for a river rescue with three drones streaming behind her.

Maledict spent her absence testing the stair alarm and every panel within reach. Pickle’s credentials opened food drawers, the courtyard, and the pet gate to the bedroom corridor. They did not open the counterseal safe. The lock override in his collar would manage that after the household quieted.

He climbed onto Brightguard’s angular field chair to wait.

She returned at three twenty, wet to the shoulders and carrying a cracked drone under one arm. “Off.”

Maledict did not move.

“That seat pinches your left hip. You complain all night afterward.”

He stayed out of principle until she reached for the health scanner. Then he descended.

“Use the bed I spent an irresponsible amount of money on.”

Under the stairs, a broad orthopedic bed occupied a climate-controlled nook. Its foam sloped beneath the hips. A heated layer held the surface at twenty-seven degrees. The slate blanket had been worn soft in the center and reinforced at one corner for digging. Water stood in three bowls because Pickle apparently held opinions about depth.

Maledict put one paw on the foam. It yielded and then supported him. He stepped fully onto it, circled once because the dog body expected to, and lay down only to assess the material.

Brightguard sat on the floor to repair her drone. Without looking up, she reached over and drew a brush along his back. The bed warmed his ribs. The brush found a knot near his shoulder, worked it loose, and moved on.

No one had placed a throne at the correct temperature.

Maledict closed his eyes for a diagnostic interval. When he opened them, the city display read 4:07.

Brightguard had repaired the drone. She rolled the red ball into the hall. “Orbit.”

Maledict intercepted it before it reached the kitchen island and returned it neatly.

“You run around the island. And you do not return it. Those are the only rules.”

He took the shortest path again.

Brightguard folded her arms. “You love this game because you cheat at the far corner. Go around.”

The third roll awakened a curve in Pickle’s legs. Maledict let the body follow it, raced around the island, and stole the ball behind a stool before Brightguard could reach the other side. When she reversed direction, he doubled back. Her old knee brace clicked; his nails scattered on the timber; the ball squealed between his teeth.

“That,” she said, pointing at him, “is orbit.”

The fourth roll was harder. Maledict improved the corner. By the eighth, he had added a feint beside the pantry. By the twelfth, Brightguard was laughing and he had forgotten that the game began as cover.

Across the city, the butler discovered that belly rubs were the only dependable method of keeping Maledict’s human body away from the windows.

Pickle lay on a laboratory rug, long legs splayed, while the butler rubbed the center of Maledict’s tailored shirt with one hand and issued tower orders with the other. Every time he stopped, a human palm struck his sleeve.

“The perimeter is sealed,” the butler told the collar channel. “Your body has eaten food appropriate to its present judgment, swallowed no artifacts, and sustained no injury. The west circle will be ready at midnight.”

Pickle’s heel beat the rug.

The butler resumed rubbing. “I also request that you be punctual.”

Maledict listened from the heated bed while Brightguard divided a liver knot into exact evening portions. Punctuality had been one of his virtues. It remained one, in principle.

At eight, Brightguard ate dinner at the low table and offered Pickle his usual pumpkin. Maledict held out for cucumber until she frowned at him, then took both. At nine, she brushed his teeth with poultry paste. At ten, she split a dental braid because the whole one was “a tomorrow problem.” At eleven, she opened the courtyard and waited under an umbrella while he inspected the rain.

Every indulgence had existed before Maledict arrived. The labeled food, the heated foam, the repaired blanket, the warm towels, the games—none was payment for abandoning his plan. Pickle had already possessed all of it. Maledict had merely infiltrated the correct life.

At eleven forty-six, the collar gave its first silent warning.

Brightguard lowered the bed temperature by one degree and pointed to the nook. “Bed.”

Maledict settled onto the foam. He waited until her steps reached the upper floor, then removed the lock override from beneath the collar lining and climbed the stairs.

The pet gate admitted him to the bedroom corridor. The counterseal safe stood behind a reinforced panel beside Brightguard’s bed. Its outer sensor recognized Pickle and disabled the pet alarm; the inner lock yielded to Maledict’s override. Inside, the pale counterseal rested in a charging frame. Touching it to the override would copy its live code to his skyscraper. The poison capsule slid from another shielded pocket in the collar, sealed and ready.

Brightguard slept on her side, silver hair darkened by the room. Her rescue brace stood beside the bed. Maledict placed the counterseal against the transmitter until a green point appeared. The code was his. He nudged the poison capsule toward her bare wrist.

The collar warmed at midnight.

Across the Tri-City Area, the west circle lit around Pickle in Maledict’s body. The butler held the climbing rope above the silver boundary and kept both of Pickle’s human feet inside. In Brightguard’s room, a small plate folded inward from Maledict’s collar. Five seconds of pressure would restore both minds. He could touch the poison, bite the plate, and wake in his skyscraper before Brightguard’s alarms understood what had happened.

His white forepaw pressed into the mattress for balance.

Brightguard’s eyes opened. “Pickle?”

Maledict froze over the poison.

She pushed herself upright and looked toward the stairs. “You never come up after dark. Your hip hates the climb.”

The return plate pulsed against his neck.

Brightguard moved her brace and cleared the low upholstered bench beside the bed. “If tonight is different, use that. I’m not lifting you after a rescue shift.”

She turned back the blanket and made a space without reaching for him.

Maledict looked at the waking hero, the counterseal, and the place she had cleared. Killing her would return him to meetings, armor, deadlines, and a throne with no heating element. The public already feared him. His organization was already obeying his absence. Nothing in the definition of ultimate evil required uncomfortable housing.

He pushed the poison into its shielded pocket. He returned the counterseal to its charging frame and nosed the safe closed. Then he used the bench.

Brightguard caught his collar as he stepped onto the mattress. “Easy. White paw first.”

He gave her the white paw. She guided him over her legs and settled back.

The plate pulsed through the last five seconds. Maledict kept his teeth away from it.

At the skyscraper, Pickle stood within the blazing circle, eyes fixed on the rope. One silver arc reached for its missing half and vanished. The laboratory went dark.

The butler lowered the rope. “We missed the window.”

Pickle took it and ran.

Brightguard draped one arm over Maledict’s borrowed ribs. “Tomorrow,” she muttered, already half asleep, “we discuss the stairs.”

Maledict put his nose on her spare pillow. Brightguard remained alive as an incidental cost of his improved circumstances.

At the next midnight, twenty-four hours after the first failed restoration, the butler charged the west circle again.

“Body safe,” his message read inside the collar display. “Tower secure. Activate on signal.”

Maledict was on Pickle’s established heated bed, eating the smaller half of a liver knot while Brightguard insisted the portions were equal. He let the signal expire.

The following afternoon, Brightguard found him on the couch.

“You never use furniture.”

Maledict stretched farther across the cushions.

“Your hip.”

He glanced at the scanner on her wrist, descended, and shoved the orthopedic bed two feet closer to the command wall. Brightguard watched him do it. Then she moved its power cord, returned the heat to twenty-seven, and went back to searching public reports for Maledict.

Nobody had found him. The searches expanded from rail tunnels to rooftops, then contracted as false sightings multiplied. His organization announced strategic silence. Brightguard discussed each report in front of the culprit and never once asked the dog where the villain had gone.

At the skyscraper, the butler built a safe routine around Pickle’s borrowed body. He covered every weapon panel, replaced breakable objects with braided rope, and scheduled rooftop exercise while the building’s staff occupied lower floors. Pickle learned to place Maledict’s human hands on a marked desk when the wall display chimed. He could not speak and never pretended to understand the calls; he watched the butler’s food pocket, wagged a tail he no longer possessed, and sometimes completed Maledict’s terrifying hand signal before chasing a reflection.

The butler kept him fed, brushed, exercised, and unharmed. He also sacrificed four shoes.

His messages shortened with each prepared return.

“West circle ready. Midnight.”

Then: “Body safe. Activate.”

Then: “Circle live.”

Brightguard’s corrections shortened too, but they kept changing Maledict’s day.

“Orbit goes around.”

He went around.

“Bath does not mean sprint toward me.”

He slowed to a walk.

“Off the field chair.”

He chose the heated bed before she raised the scanner.

She added cucumber to the snack shelf without removing the salmon. She placed the bedside bench permanently beside the mattress. When Maledict failed the old greeting, she waited with her palm out until his white forepaw landed there; after that, she let him steal the ball any way he pleased.

On the seventh night, the butler stood beside the west circle with his jacket unbuttoned and his last intact shoe under one arm. Pickle had curled Maledict’s long human body onto a new reinforced bed in the penthouse, knees drawn up, cheek pressed against the stolen shoe. The roof controls were locked. The weapons were dark. No camera showed the room.

The butler opened the collar channel.

“Sir. Midnight.”

Across the Tri-City Area, Maledict lay in the worn center of Pickle’s original bed. Brightguard had finished the brushing, checked his left hip, and left two salmon coins on the edge of the snack cabinet for morning. The floor held at twenty-seven degrees.

The plate warmed beneath his collar.

From the stairs, Brightguard said, “White paw under the blanket. It’s cold tonight.”

Maledict tucked the naturally white forepaw beneath the slate-blue edge.

The butler’s signal pulsed until the window closed.

stories.title: The Cat Who Had Enough
stories.prompt: you inherit a magic cat that gives advice about life when you complain to it. However, one day it snaps, giving you a long frustrated lecture about how much of a waste you are and that you are the source of your own problems
stories.body:
# The Cat Who Had Enough

Tallow came to me through Aunt Beryl's will, although not in the way the phrase inherited a cat suggests.

I received a blue ceramic dish, a modest account marked FOR TALLOW'S EXPENSES, and two typed notes. The first said that Tallow was a living companion, not an item, and that I should ask whether he wanted to stay with me. The second explained his one unusual faculty. If I complained directly to him, he could choose to answer in human speech about that complaint. He could keep answering while the grievance remained the subject. Anything else came out as a rusty meow.

At thirty-two, I considered myself capable of making a cat feel welcome without written guidance. Tallow considered my apartment for one slow circuit, sniffed the food I offered, and went to sleep on my cleanest chair. He stayed.

His first advice arrived before I had put Beryl's notes away.

I had locked the door, put down three bags, and discovered that my keys were no longer in either hand. After searching the bags twice, I addressed the broad charcoal cat washing a white paw beside the skirting board.

“Tallow, this apartment hides my keys the moment I come inside.”

His paw stopped beside his ear. “Drop them in Beryl's blue dish every time you enter.”

The dish sat on the hall table directly below my elbow.

“The issue isn't where keys could theoretically go. The issue is catching the transition between outside mode and inside mode.”

Tallow looked at the door, then at the dish. “Your hand passes over it when you turn the lock.”

This was practical but insufficiently responsive to the kind of person I was. I needed a solution with positive capture. That night I ordered a brass hook shaped like an antler, after rejecting nickel as too temporary and black iron as falsely rustic.

The hook arrived with three kinds of wall anchor. Since I did not know whether the wall was plaster, masonry, or an innovative hybrid, I left the hook sealed in its padded envelope on the hall table while I researched diagnostic tapping.

Four days later I found my keys in yesterday's coat. I had searched that coat while wearing it.

The blue dish remained empty under the envelope.

During the second week, healthy eating became structurally impossible.

“Tallow, every sensible recipe assumes I have six prepared ingredients and the temperament to chop a squash on a Wednesday.”

He had been asleep in a stripe of sun on the kitchen floor. One ear came upright; the rest of him did not.

“Buy eggs, bread, and three vegetables you already eat. Cook one before you buy more.”

“That's provisioning, not nutrition. I need a repeatable food practice.”

“Repeat the eggs.”

Instead, I ordered ten stackable glass tubs with bamboo lids. Their product photographs showed a refrigerator arranged by color, season, and moral seriousness. I also bought spinach, fennel, radishes, beetroot, two cabbages, fresh turmeric, and a rosemary plant. The eggs seemed uninspired after that, so I left them at the shop.

The tubs remained in their cardboard sleeves because I had not decided whether to label them by ingredient, meal, or date. The vegetables remained in their bags because washing them before I had settled the tub question would have been premature.

By Friday, the spinach had become damp green paper. The fennel had grown a brown thumb.

“Tallow, shops package produce for imaginary households.”

Tallow sat beside his bowl and looked past me at the unopened tubs.

“Eggs,” he said.

“That doesn't engage with the packaging issue.”

He lowered his face to his food. The conversation was apparently over, although the complaint technically was not.

The third week belonged to laundry. The washer completed its work with three discreet chimes, all inaudible from my desk. I left one load wet overnight, washed it again, and left it wet through lunch.

“Tallow, a machine shouldn't depend on a human remembering when the machine has finished.”

He was curled on the towels I had not yet put away. “Set one alarm when you press start. Stand up when it rings.”

“A single alert has no resilience.”

“It needs obedience, not resilience.”

I designed four alarms: Cycle Expected, Cycle Check, Laundry Transition, and Final Laundry Safeguard. Choosing distinct sounds took twenty minutes. Then I bought lavender scent beads, because a reliable habit needs an attractive reward.

On Saturday, Cycle Expected interrupted me while I was changing the icon for Cycle Check. Laundry Transition arrived during a video about notification fatigue. I dismissed Final Laundry Safeguard on principle because the first three had made it redundant.

The load waited in the dark drum until Sunday morning.

“Tallow, the clothes smell worse than before I washed them.”

He had retreated to the top shelf of the linen cupboard, as far from the damp drum as the cupboard allowed. His eyes stayed shut.

“Alarm.”

“There were four alarms.”

“One. Then move.”

I restarted the machine with extra detergent and two caps of scent beads. On the shelf above it, I left the tea that had accompanied my alarm design. Honey dried around the teaspoon in the bottom of the cup.

By the fourth week, Tallow's advice had shortened enough that I began to worry he was losing professional curiosity.

The rule did not let him answer that question. “Tallow, are you bored?” earned only a rusty meow. I tried again: “Tallow, it is frustrating that I can't tell whether you're bored.”

“Stop waking me to ask.”

This seemed sharp at the time, so I wrote it in a notebook titled Tallow's Observations.

That same week, I addressed him on the windowsill. “Tallow, money escapes through charges too small to deserve individual attention.”

“Open your statement. Cancel the first recurring charge you don't use.”

“Statements are retrospective. I need something that reveals the pattern early.”

I found a budgeting app whose blue graphs made spending look like a weather system. It promised to locate subscriptions automatically after I linked my accounts. The free trial became $7.99 a month, but setup took only ten minutes, and ten minutes of financial administration deserved the first clean part of a morning, not the dented quarter-hour before lunch.

I put my coffee on the windowsill while reading its reviews. The cup stayed there with the teaspoon inside.

When the app renewed, I tried again. “Tallow, now I have two petty charges instead of one.”

Tallow opened his eyes.

“Statement.”

“I know what a statement is.”

“Open.”

His tail covered his nose. No amount of elaboration drew out a third word.

In week five, my wireless headphones died halfway through a program about reducing friction at home. The charging cable lay plugged in beside my right hand, looped around the pot of a dead rosemary plant so it could not fall behind the desk.

“Tallow, nothing in this apartment is ever charged when I need it.”

He occupied the only rectangle of warm sunlight on the desk. His gaze moved from the headphones to the cable.

“Plug them in.”

“The cable is technically available, but it has no permanent relationship to the headphones.”

“It is touching them.”

I ordered a premium charging dock for my phone, headphones, and a watch I did not own. It arrived in a matte white box that made loose wires seem like a social class I had escaped. Its natural position was Tallow's rectangle of sun, so I set the unopened box there temporarily while I considered the ethics of permanent placement.

The headphones remained beside their cable, uncharged.

While researching cable channels, I brought another coffee to the desk and put it beside the old cup. Both cups now held teaspoons. I used a third spoon to pry open the battery cover of my kitchen scale, carried it with me when the scale failed to solve a question about portioning, and pushed it upright into the rosemary pot so it would not mark the desk.

Tallow watched all three journeys. When I told him the headphones still refused to stay ready, he turned once on the chair and settled with his back to me.

“Cable,” he said into his own flank.

The sixth week began with a Sunday-reset binder and spread into pantry review, hydration tracking, and a bathroom skin-care trial. Preparation made me thirsty. Two cups of tea reached the sofa on saucers, each with a spoon; one saucer slid under the binder when I opened it wide. During the pantry review, I set a teaspoon in the jar labeled GRAINS, alongside three buttons and an old receipt. I ate yogurt from the carton and left it open beside the full kitchen bin, the spoon standing in it like a small flag. In the bathroom, I mixed a green face mask with another teaspoon.

By Saturday night, three more teaspoons lay in the sink: one from instant coffee, one from jam, and one from a cup of tea I had carried as far as the kitchen before deciding that counted as clearing up.

Tallow followed these routes with his eyes. I thought he was fascinated by teaspoons. It did not occur to me that he was counting.

On the sixth Sunday, sunlight lay cleanly across the kitchen tiles. Tallow ate fish from his shallow bowl. I put bread in the toaster, boiled water, and opened the cutlery drawer.

The teaspoon slot was empty.

I felt under the forks, checked the drying rack, and pulled the drawer farther out in case twelve spoons had slipped behind it in formation. Three were visible in the sink, but they looked used in a way that excluded them from the category I needed.

“Tallow, this apartment eats teaspoons. A functional home shouldn't demand constant surveillance of its own cutlery.”

He stopped chewing.

“Retrieve the twelve teaspoons you carried away,” he said. “Wash them.”

“You have answered the literal problem while missing the larger one.”

Tallow lifted his head. A flake of fish clung to one whisker.

“The larger one,” I said, “is that life consists of hundreds of tiny maintenance demands, and if a person has to consciously manage every—”

“No.” He stepped over his bowl. “You do not get to inflate twelve dirty spoons into the human condition before I finish breakfast.”

He sprang onto the counter. His tail struck the cupboard once.

“Three are in that sink. I watched you drop them there: coffee, jam, tea. Number four is planted in the yogurt carton beside a bin so full that the lid is balancing on an orange peel. You will say those four are not missing because you can see them. That is worse. Your apartment has not eaten your teaspoons. It has been forced to exhibit them.”

“I was going to clear—”

“After breakfast, after the reset, after a fresh morning. Yes. I know the calendar of never.”

He jumped down and walked out of the kitchen. I followed; six weeks of compressed answers had acquired alarming momentum.

In the hall, Tallow put his white paw on Beryl's blue dish. It rocked against the table. The padded envelope underneath rustled.

“Here is your first emergency. Beryl placed a dish where your hand passes after locking the door. You declared it passive and bought a brass antler. It has spent forty days sealed in this envelope while you researched the wall without tapping it and compared anchors without opening them. The dish asked for one movement. The hook asked for money, wall analysis, and a drill, so you called it better. It has caught no keys. It has only pinned the useful dish under its backside.”

“The wall could genuinely be—”

“Plaster, brick, or cheese. I heard the keys jingle when you hung that coat yesterday; they are in the pocket. Do not reach for them yet. We are touring your achievements.”

He trotted to my desk. The charging dock had flattened one corner of its own box where Tallow had repeatedly tried to sit on it. He leaped beside the dead rosemary, sniffed its dry stems, and recoiled from the old coffee cups.

“Number five is in your rosemary pot. You pried at a battery cover, carried the spoon from the kitchen, and buried it here. Six and seven are in these cups: one in old milk, one in instant coffee and vanilla powder.

“Here is the cable: six inches, plugged in, touching the dead headphones. Here is the premium dock you will not unpack until the room reveals its eternal form. You bought space for three devices, including a watch you do not own, and blocked my sun with the box. Cats find the warm patch before it moves. You research where to put the warmth.”

I opened my mouth.

“You were about to invoke good design. Yours has prevented charging and naps in matte white packaging.”

He crossed the keyboard. The budgeting app was still open on the screen behind a prompt asking me to link my first account.

“There is the machine you hired to notice money. It noticed $7.99 and took it. The original charge remains; the app is the second. You paid your solution to join the problem.”

“The trial terms weren't prominent.”

“They were prominent enough for you to quote the star rating. You refused a statement because it had already happened, then bought a blue graph that would describe it later. You want knowledge decorated and innocent of any demand.”

Tallow dropped to the sofa. He nosed the Sunday-reset binder aside, revealing one saucer, then stared at the other.

“Eight. Nine. Two teas made to accompany the plan for returning things to their places. One spoon went under the plan. The other stayed in full view. You call this reset because abandonment sounded insufficiently branded.”

On his way toward the laundry cupboard, he paused at the bathroom door.

“Number ten is beside the sink in a bowl of green paste.”

“That one wasn't used for food.”

“There it is. Change the assignment and the spoon leaves the count. The keys become a transition problem, the spinach a packaging failure, the wet clothes a communications defect. You promote objects into concepts until they are unavailable for ordinary work.”

He reached the laundry cupboard, where the machine held a load I had remembered this time only because I needed the shirt at the top. The honeyed cup remained on the shelf above it.

“Number eleven. Old honey, damp cotton, and enough lavender to erase a small bird. You needed one alarm and made four. You dismissed one while choosing an icon, one while hearing why alarms fail, and two because the others annoyed you. Then you blamed the machine and washed the load again with double detergent. You gave laundry the afternoon, the night, and my linen shelf.”

His back fur had risen into a charcoal ridge. He turned and marched to the kitchen without checking whether I followed.

“I know what comes next,” he called. “Systems are oppressive; your mind needs a personal one. You will call me categorical while filing everything under Not My Fault. You spent forty minutes comparing unopened tubs. Fairness will not wash spoons.”

Back in the kitchen, he jumped onto the counter beside the unopened tubs. Through the refrigerator door came the sweet, damp smell of vegetables returning themselves to soil.

“Number twelve is in the jar marked GRAINS, among three buttons and a receipt. The jar contains no grain. Your glass tubs are still wrapped. Spinach collapsed, fennel browned, radishes softened, and the cabbages survived because cabbages are built for sieges. You bought food for a disciplined stranger, ordered noodles when the stranger failed to arrive, and blamed the quantities.

“Do you understand what a waste you are?”

Heat climbed into my face. “That's a needlessly—”

“Specific word? It is the first one broad enough. You are a waste. You waste food, water, detergent, scent beads, fees, packaging, mornings, clear surfaces, and every answer after demanding it. You preserve Beryl's useful dish beneath its useless replacement. You block my warm places with unopened equipment and interrupt my naps with mysteries I watched your hands create.

“You waste an entirely operational intelligence. You can compare anchor strengths, bamboo-lid care, alert architecture, app reviews, and cable channels. You can build an argument against moving your hand six inches. You can make a spoon sound like weather. All that cleverness manufactures an alibi for the person present along the whole route.

“You are the source of these problems: manufacturer, distributor, and most loyal customer. Your hands placed every spoon. Your thumb dismissed every alarm. Your card bought every substitute. Your feet passed the dish. Then cause reaches consequence and you introduce them as strangers.

“You ask for advice as if novelty were action. I began with sentences, shortened them, and finally gave you nouns: eggs, alarm, statement, cable. The advice did not become inadequate. My patience became accurate. You wanted fresh answers to admire while preserving the complaints that summoned me.

“I am done donating sleep to that arrangement. Wash the spoons. Eat what you buy. Move the laundry when the alarm rings. Open the statement. Connect the headphones. Put the keys in the dish. The dish is under the envelope. The cable is beside the headphones. Stop shopping between yourself and the verb.

“Now get number twelve out of the button jar and stop accusing the apartment of having a mouth.”

Tallow stopped speaking. The toaster released my bread with a dry click. He returned to his bowl; the fish had gone tacky around the edges. He ate it anyway, fast and offended.

I collected the spoons.

Three came from the sink and one from the yogurt carton. The rosemary pot gave up its little metal marker; the two windowsill cups gave up theirs. I found two on the sofa, one with the binder's square imprint in a ring of tea. Green paste had dried on the bathroom spoon. The laundry spoon required hot water to loosen the honey. The jar marked GRAINS supplied the last among the buttons and receipt.

Twelve teaspoons made a surprisingly small heap beside the tap.

I nearly told Tallow that cleaning all of them at once would consume the morning. His left ear turned toward me before I made the first word.

I filled the basin. The yogurt spoon was worst. I scrubbed that one first, soaked the honeyed one, rinsed the rest, and put all twelve in the drying rack.

That afternoon, I reached the front door and found my keys absent from both hands. The blue dish was empty. The brass antler still pressed down on it in its padded envelope.

“This apart—”

I stopped before I aimed the complaint at Tallow. He lay asleep in the strip of sun beside the boxed charging dock.

Yesterday's coat hung on the back of the chair. The keys were in its pocket.

stories.title: The First Call
stories.prompt: The kingdom laughed when a rooster marched to war in battered armor, but years later, when the last surviving soldiers saw an enormous feathered warrior emerge from the burning battlefield with arrows in his back and dawn behind him, they realized the legends had gotten one thing wrong: he had never been anyone’s mascot.
stories.body:
# The First Call

The first thing Dawnwatch asked of Tebri was a repair.

He came up the muster road before the levy horn, while cooks were still coaxing damp wood and the kingdom's newest soldiers were discovering which straps pinched. He was a red rooster, broad in the breast, marching under a suit of battered armor.

Laughter reached him from both sides of the road. It began with the spear ranks, spread through the archers, and doubled when he passed the officers' horses without breaking step. Someone crowed back at him. Someone offered odds on how long he would last in the stew pot.

Tebri did not laugh until he stopped at her bench.

His breastplate was genuine steel, dark with old oil. Overlapping scales ran from his shoulders to his tail, their edges worn bright beneath a crust of road dust. The leather under his wings had been patched with three kinds of stitching. No craftsman had fitted the whole thing, at least not in its present shape; one hinge was village work, another delicate enough for a jeweler, and a strip of copper wire held the spine together where a proper pin had been lost.

The rooster looked at Tebri, looked at the buckles arranged on her cloth, and lifted his left wing. A belly strap had twisted half around.

That was when she laughed. Not because he wore armor. Because every soldier who had ever reached her bench with a split strap had begun by telling her it was the armor's fault, and this one had simply shown her the fault.

"Stand still, then."

He did.

Tebri turned the strap flat. Its inner face was polished by long use, though the wearer beneath her hands was no larger than any farmyard cock. She punched a new hole, shortened a keeper, and tested the buckle with two fingers. The rooster shifted his weight once, settled the breastplate, and lowered his wing.

"Better?"

He struck the plate with his beak. The note rang clean.

The soldiers around the bench applauded. The rooster ignored them. He walked the length of Tebri's laid-out tools, paused over the awl she had used, then returned to the muster road.

A clerk intercepted him with the end of a roll. "Whose bird?"

"No mark," Tebri said.

The captain appeared behind the clerk, fastening his sword belt as he walked. He had one boot on and one foot wrapped in linen. "Will it march?"

The rooster was already inspecting the last rank, ducking beneath the tails of coats and stepping around packs. Twice he stopped before a man whose scabbard hung too low. The men moved them out of his way, still grinning.

"Apparently," Tebri said.

"Put him with the baggage."

A handler bent to catch him. The rooster slipped between the man's boots, crossed behind the column, and took a place on the road precisely one pace beyond the final soldier.

The captain watched him refuse a second pair of hands. "Mascot, then. Mascots don't need formation space."

"No one asked what he needs."

The captain glanced at the unsounded horn, the waiting levy, and his bare foot. "I need the army moving. Clerk, write 'red rooster, mascot' and give the quartermaster a number."

The clerk dipped his pen. "Name?"

The rooster threw back his head and crowed.

It was a deep, carrying call. The horses along the picket tossed their heads; cooks looked up from their smoke; the officer holding the levy horn lowered it in surprise. For one breath the entire field listened to the rooster's call instead.

The clerk wrote Dawnwatch.

Only after Dawnwatch had walked past every rank and wagon did he resume his place at the rear. The horn sounded late. He marched when the soldiers marched, beneath armor that had known other roads.

Within a month he belonged to every story the company told about itself.

He slept under Tebri's fitting bench, where falling sparks died on the packed earth before they reached him. He cleared weevils from the flour. His shed feathers kept grain beetles away, though they also bleached every red-dyed thing they touched to orange. The quartermaster lined the bins with feathers, then came to Tebri waving a mottled cuff.

"That bird has eaten half my flour and ruined a good coat."

"He ate what was eating the flour."

"I can dislike two creatures at once."

Dawnwatch opened one eye beneath the bench. The quartermaster tucked three more feathers into his sleeve before leaving.

He learned the company's calls, or perhaps he had known calls before theirs. He came to the short note for rations but ignored the one used for mules. He moved on the marching horn, halted on the double fall, and on inspection days walked the ranks ahead of the captain. The soldiers began tying bits of ribbon to his back plates. Dawnwatch removed each ribbon and left it in Tebri's scrap bowl.

They called that pride in his costume.

Tebri called him fussy, because fussy things were familiar. He would not enter his harness if a buckle lay crooked. If a scale caught the grain of his feathers, he gripped her sleeve and drew her hand to the spot. He never struck flesh. He waited until she understood, then tested the repair by sound.

The first wet season put them on a border road drowned between willow marshes. Rain erased the road's edges and filled every wheel rut to the color of iron. The baggage master built Dawnwatch a dry perch under the canvas. Dawnwatch stepped off it and climbed the bare rise where the forward sentry stood.

Tebri followed with an oilcloth, meaning to cover the fresh patch on his back.

The sentry leaned on his spear. "Your little officer wants the high ground."

Dawnwatch faced the willows instead of the road. Rain slicked his comb flat. He did not look at Tebri when she spread the cloth.

"What is it?" she asked.

His head tipped left. Beyond the rain, nothing moved except long leaves.

The sentry laughed. "Ask him where the enemy is while you're at it."

Dawnwatch gave three short crows.

The first silenced the sentry. The second turned him toward the willows. Before the third ended, Tebri saw a branch rise against the wind. Someone was passing beneath it.

She dropped the oilcloth and ran downhill shouting, "Willows!"

The hidden bowmen loosed before the captain had the shield rank closed. Arrows punched the baggage canvas. A frightened mule pulled the lead wagon crosswise, blocking the road behind them. Men crowded against the flooded ditch while more shapes moved through the willows.

Dawnwatch came down the rise into that confusion. He struck twice at the mouth of a charcoal track so narrow Tebri had mistaken it for runoff, then dragged one spur through the mud in a line toward the trees.

The sentry went first. The shield rank followed because there was no room to argue. Tebri cut the trapped mule loose while soldiers shouldered the wagon aside, and the company escaped between smoking charcoal pits before the hidden force closed the road.

Dawnwatch remained beside the track mouth until the last cart turned. He came after it with an arrow groove through three back scales and blood darkening the feathers beneath his right wing.

He refused Tebri's hands until the captain had called the roll. Only when the final answer came did he crouch on her folded coat.

By supper, the warning had become luck. Dawnwatch had climbed the hill to hunt worms. Dawnwatch's crow had startled the ambushers into moving too soon. Dawnwatch had scratched at the track because all roosters scratched, and the company had been clever enough to understand.

The sentry repeated those versions loudest.

Tebri set the damaged scales on her bench. "You saw him watching the trees."

"I saw him being a rooster," the sentry said. He could not meet her eyes. "And I followed. Both can be true."

She had no answer that would improve the metal. She cut a replacement from the blue cuff of a ruined vambrace, rounded the edge, and fitted it where the arrow had struck. Dawnwatch listened to its note. When Tebri reached for a punch to stamp the company's little crown into the plate, he put his foot over it.

"Not ours?" she asked.

His claws remained on the blank steel.

She left it blank.

The second winter reduced the company to the smell of wet wool and the nightly recitation of names. Men slept with heated stones in their blankets and woke to stones cold enough to burn their palms. Dawnwatch's comb went pale at the tips. Tebri made him a lined cover for the armor; he tolerated it in camp and shook it off before every march.

One evening the count came back complete. Forty-six walking, five carried, no one missing.

Dawnwatch did not eat.

He paced from the ration pan to the dark road, struck the pan once, and returned to the road. When Tebri blocked him, he tugged the ring on her lantern.

"The count is good."

He went six paces into the snow and waited.

"The count is good," she said again, because the wind had begun filling their own tracks.

Dawnwatch came back, struck the lantern ring, and walked away a second time.

Tebri took the lantern. At the edge of camp she told the sentry, "If I am not back by the watch change, tell the captain his mascot has stolen his armorer."

Dawnwatch led her nearly half a mile. He left the road where a drift had buried the ditch and began digging with both feet. Tebri heard nothing until she knelt and pressed her ear to the snow. Beneath it, someone breathed in thin, broken pulls.

The missing spearman had answered at roll and wandered off afterward, fevered and snow-blind. One hand was wedged under his pack. Tebri dug until her fingers went numb. Dawnwatch crouched beside the small air hole and spread his wings across it, keeping loose snow from falling into the man's face.

They hauled him back on Tebri's coat. Dawnwatch walked beside his head, stopping whenever the man's breathing changed. At camp he ignored grain and warmth until the surgeon forced broth between the spearman's teeth.

The man's hands survived, except for the tips of two fingers. The story did not. By morning, the company had decided Dawnwatch had smelled his favorite soldier through the storm. By spring, some versions said the rooster had dragged the man free himself.

Tebri widened both belly straps after that winter. Dawnwatch had not grown, but the armor kept needing room in places that did not touch his body. She began recording every alteration on a strip of hide in her tool roll.

"You counted after the roll," she said while he stood on the bench.

Dawnwatch watched her select a drill.

"You knew one was gone."

He picked up the narrow chisel in his beak and set it beside her hand.

The chisel was better suited to the rivet. Tebri used it. She still wrote mascot on the repair docket, because the quartermaster accepted repairs for mascots and asked questions about armor made for soldiers.

Six years passed by changing the suit.

The copper wire vanished beneath a black steel bridge. Tebri replaced buckles, shortened straps, lengthened the same straps, and once found a sword cut in a place no rooster hiding under a wagon could have earned. The blue scales multiplied across Dawnwatch's right shoulder. Fewer soldiers remembered the muster. The ones who joined later knew him first as the lucky bird in the old stories.

Then a drill broke through what Tebri had always thought was padding.

An outer plate lifted from the breastpiece. Beneath it lay a second plate folded along a joint so fine it had gathered no rust. Another waited beneath that one, and another, nested like metal feathers. Their inner faces carried broad, smooth wear marks, each as wide as Tebri's palm. The leather she had believed too thick was doubled and turned inward around empty space.

She removed three rivets. The back assembly loosened and revealed a black pin at its center, dull as quenched iron and untouched by six years of weather. Old tool marks scarred the socket. None were hers.

Tebri reached for pliers.

Dawnwatch knocked them from her hand.

The blow was hard enough to send the tool under the bench. He planted both feet on the open harness. His feathers lifted; his amber eye stayed fixed on hers.

"That pin locks all of it," Tebri said. "If it shifts, the spine may open."

He struck the black head once.

"Yes. I see it."

He placed one foot over the pin.

Not this tool, then. Or not this day. Tebri sat back on her heels. Around them, twelve soldiers did the camp work that thirty had shared at the beginning of the war. The cookfires were small. The captain's new orders waited under a stone, sending the company toward another road people had already failed to hold.

"Were you this size when someone made it?"

Dawnwatch stepped off the harness.

"Did they call you something else?"

He raised his left wing, exposing the belly strap.

Tebri almost laughed. Instead she closed the hidden plates and entered only "backplate rivets" on the repair docket. Mascots could be ordered under a wagon; whatever had worn those inner plates could not. By morning she had convinced herself the distinction was practical.

At dawn he took the forward half of the column.

The last evening of the company began when Tebri's own side burned its supply carts.

They fired two to keep them from capture. An enemy arrow carried flame to the third. Oil ran across the road, and the road became a bright wall between the rearguard and the retreating army. Horns called from both sides of the smoke. One signaled withdrawal. Another insisted on holding ground no one could see.

Tebri came through with the captain's weight on her left shoulder and her tool pack cutting into the right. His leg dragged uselessly. Behind them, arrows ticked off iron rims and disappeared into fire.

Dawnwatch emerged from beneath a wagon, feathers black with soot. Blood showed in a narrow line below the oldest side plate.

"With me," Tebri coughed.

He ran the other way.

Eight soldiers had reached the unburned verge: the bowwoman, the spearman from the winter ditch, four others, Tebri, and the captain. The spearman carried the furled standard under one arm. All of them watched the smoke for shapes that did not come.

Dawnwatch crossed to a weed-grown lane bending away from the main road. He struck its stones twice and cut a line in the ash behind him.

The bowwoman saw first. "He found a turn."

"We don't know where it goes," Tebri said.

"We know where this goes."

Arrows landed along the verge. The captain tried to stand on his bad leg and folded. Dawnwatch repeated the two strikes, then disappeared down the lane.

They followed.

The lane ended at a stone culvert beneath an old field wall. Dawnwatch tore dead grass from its mouth. The opening was too low for anyone carrying the captain, so Tebri and the bowwoman pushed him through on Tebri's leather apron and crawled after him. Beyond the wall, a drainage cut ran parallel to the road, deep enough to hide them if they stayed below its rim.

Dawnwatch walked its length, touching one boot, knee, or hand from each survivor. At the far end he listened toward the road. Then he turned back to the culvert.

Tebri caught the rear of his harness. "You've done it. Come on."

He leaned forward. His claws found holds in the mud. There was no frightened beating of wings, only steady pressure against her grip.

The bowwoman lifted her head above the bank and dropped at once. "They're spreading from the wagons. Two along our side."

Tebri picked Dawnwatch up. His injured leg shook against her wrist. "We can carry him between the bows."

The spearman unrolled the edge of the standard. "Use this."

Dawnwatch allowed Tebri to loosen the first belly buckle. At the second, he twisted free, drove his beak against the black pin, and faced the culvert.

Pin. Culvert. Then a black scratch drawn across the ditch in the direction the survivors needed to travel.

Tebri stared at him.

He did it again.

"No. That is the lock for every hidden plate. If I cut it, I cannot promise the harness will close."

Dawnwatch set one foot toward the culvert.

The captain, flat on the apron, opened his eyes. "Can he hold them?"

"I don't know what he can do."

Dawnwatch struck the pin.

The bowwoman said, "They've found the lane."

Voices carried through the culvert now. Someone pushed grass aside at its far mouth. Tebri pulled at the shoulder buckle, trying to strip the harness off and hide him under a coat.

Dawnwatch caught the web of her hand in his beak.

He did not bite down. He held her until she stopped.

For six years Tebri had known the exact pressure he would accept under each wing. She knew which old scar made him shorten one step and which plate he tested twice in rain. She had read every choice he made as information when it concerned metal. Beyond her bench, she had let the company turn the same precision into luck.

Dawnwatch released her hand and lowered his body before the black pin.

Tebri took the narrow chisel from her pack.

"Hold," she said.

He became still.

She set the edge into the old tool marks. The first hammer stroke chipped the socket. The second drove the pin sideways. At the third, the black metal split.

Every hidden plate moved.

The breastpiece opened in long sections across Dawnwatch's chest. Back scales slid outward, blue patches racing apart as older steel unfolded between them. Springs released with the shriek of drawn blades. The harness filled the ditch from wall to wall.

Dawnwatch rose inside it.

His legs lengthened and planted deeper in the mud. Red feathers spread through the widening armor; shoulders lifted above Tebri's head; the small wings she had bandaged in winter opened into vast feathered arms. He drove upward against the interlocking plates as if straightening after years spent bent.

At the culvert, an enemy face appeared between the grasses.

Dawnwatch turned. The full movement of him sent smoke and ash rolling back through the opening. He stepped over the field wall and vanished onto the burning road beyond the culvert.

Tebri heard a bowstring. Then many. Metal rang. A wingbeat struck the air hard enough to flatten grass along the ditch, followed by men shouting to one another through the fire.

The bowwoman seized Tebri's shoulder. "Move."
