The heaven train vanished into the black beyond the station.

In my pocket, the ticket burned cold.

I pulled it out. The outer of its two borders had faded from black to gray.
The film still hid the destination.

“That route has lapsed,” Hester said behind me.

The hell board read:

**HELL — 5 MINUTES**

***

Sabine came to the window opposite me.

Smoke moved across the glass between us, thinning and thickening. When it
cleared, I saw the pressure marks the luggage rail had left across her palms.
She held up her ticket. Its destination field remained ash gray around the
unchanged black word HELL.

“Can she get out?” I asked.

“I have not seen anyone get out after a transfer,” Hester said.

“You knew that would happen.”

“I warned you that I had seen it happen.”

“You could have stopped us.”

“I could not have stopped the train. I might have tried to restrain her. Or
you.” Hester looked at Sabine rather than at me. “I did not.”

The answer gave me no clean place to put my anger.

The platform gate beneath the hell sign stood closed, its brass plate dark.
Heat lifted from the train in dry, unsteady waves. Behind Sabine, the carriage
was dim but material: wooden benches, leather straps, brass bolts dulled almost
green. I could not see who else sat there. I could not see what waited beyond
the tunnel.

“If I board it,” I asked, “will it take me?”

“Present your ticket and the gate will respond.”

“That isn’t an answer.”

“It is what I know.”

“What if mine says heaven?”

“That service has gone.”

The words struck harder than the iron noise. If Asha was anywhere beyond that
warm carriage—if the scent had been more than memory, if there had been even
the smallest chance—I had let it leave. No punishment could be as precise as
not knowing whether I had missed her.

The board clicked to three minutes.

“And if mine says hell?”

Hester’s gaze fell to the covered field. “Then the label would match this
train. I cannot tell you whether the label is just. I cannot tell you what the
destination contains.”

I could peel the film and surrender to whichever sentence waited beneath. If
it said hell, I could call boarding honesty, or punishment, or the courage I
had failed to show beside Asha. If it said heaven, I could spend whatever
remained knowing that absolution had once been offered and that I had thrown it
away.

Both fantasies asked the station to finish my guilt for me.

Sabine struck the glass once.

The sound was muffled, but I flinched. She did not point to the closed gate or
beckon me toward the train. She only looked at me. The fury in her face was
not a message about my destination. It belonged to her.

I went close enough that the heat tightened my skin.

“I helped you because I wanted you to prove it could be escaped,” I said. “I
wanted you to find out for me.”

Sabine’s mouth moved. The window gave me no sound.

“I’m sorry.”

I did not ask whether she forgave me.

The final minute disappeared from the board. A warning bell rang inside the
hell train. Its doors folded shut.

Hester said, “If you let this service leave, the other border will lapse. I
have seen no later train here accept a ticket after that.”

My hand closed around the paper. I wanted to open it so badly that my thumbnail
creased the black film. I wanted a word to hate. I wanted one to obey.

I kept my thumb still.

The train moved.

Sabine walked with the window as long as the carriage allowed. I walked on my
side, neither of us looking away. Her palm stayed against the glass, the blue
line around her wrist visible until smoke covered it, until the last car passed,
until the red lamps at the rear became two embers and went out.

The inner border on my ticket turned gray.

Then the ink of my name, the warning, and both borders drained into the paper.
The black peel-back film lightened last. In a few breaths I held a blank cream
rectangle.

Behind me, both passenger gates locked with the sound of bolts driven home.

***

I tried them anyway.

The heaven gate did not light when I pressed the blank ticket to its plate. The
hell gate did not light. I shook each until the brass bars rattled in their
housings.

“Another service,” I said. “You said there are other tickets. Let me take
another service.”

“Not with that ticket.”

“Give me a new one.”

“I cannot.”

“Who can?”

Hester picked up her ledger. “No one I have seen.”

The boards went dark. Without their words, the station became only tile, iron,
and the stale smell of cooling brakes. There was no revelation in it. No voice
told me that refusal was noble. My blank ticket did not become a key to
something hidden.

Hester crossed behind the information window and pressed her palm to the
painted rectangle in the wall. A narrow door opened without showing what lay
beyond; there was only a wedge of ordinary yellow light and the edge of another
gray wall.

I hurried after her. The opening narrowed before I reached it. I wedged the
blank ticket into the gap. The door pushed the paper back without bending it
and shut.

“Hester.”

She looked at me from the other side.

“How long am I here?”

“I don’t know.”

“What am I supposed to do?”

“I don’t know that either.”

The door sealed, leaving only the hairline in the paint.

I was alone.

I thought of Asha’s room after I left it: the chair pulled close to her bed,
the cup with its bent straw, the phone close enough for her to reach. I had
imagined that room so many times that memory and invention had worn into each
other. I did not know whether she had been awake when she called. I did not
know whether she had been afraid. I knew only what I had done.

I sat on the bench and placed the blank ticket beside me.

The cold worked through my clothes. There was no sunrise beyond the windows.
There was no clock now that the boards were dark. I counted my breaths until I
understood that counting would not make time answer.

Then the board mechanisms stirred.

Letters flipped into place above both tracks. New minutes appeared. The blank
ticket beside me remained blank.

At the far end of the bench, a woman gasped.

She wore wet slippers and a hospital wristband. Her hands clutched the front of
her gown closed. She stared at the boards, then at me.

“Am I dead?”

The old impulse rose whole inside me: step away before fear became a request.
Find the painted door. Find the darkest part of the platform. Let her peel her
ticket and carry whatever word waited there without making it mine.

I picked up my blank ticket and moved toward her.

“Yes,” I said.

She began to cry without sound.

I sat at the other end of the bench, leaving the seat between us open. After a
moment she crossed that space herself and caught my sleeve.

“What happens?”

“I can tell you what I’ve seen here.”

I told her about the gates and the one-service warning. I told her I did not
know who had made the labels, whether they were fair, or what waited beyond
them. When I reached Sabine, I did not say the train had taken a passenger, as
if she had been luggage. I said her name. I said I had held the door. I said I
had watched her dragged from the moving heaven train into the hell train, and
that she had remained herself all the way to the last window.

The woman listened with both hands around her unopened ticket.

“Which one was yours?” she asked.

I showed her the blank paper. “I didn’t look.”

“Can you still go?”

“The gates won’t open for me.”

She glanced toward the tracks. “Was it worth it?”

The question had no answer that would not pretend I knew more than I did.

“It was my choice,” I said. “And Sabine paid for part of it.”

The woman looked down. With one careful pull, she peeled the film from her
ticket. Her shoulders shook when she read the word, but she turned it so I
could see.

**HEAVEN**.

“Is it?” she asked. “Heaven?”

“That is where the sign says the train goes.”

“But is it?”

“I don’t know.”

The rails began their distant song. She tightened her grip on my sleeve.

“Will you stay until it comes?”

My sister’s voice did not enter the station. No warmth passed through me. There
was only this frightened stranger, the pressure of her fingers, and the
approaching light.

“Yes,” I said.

The train drew in with its clean windows and ordinary blue seats. Warm air
crossed the platform when the doors opened, carrying lemon and cotton and a
hundred other things I could have made into promises. The woman presented her
own ticket. The gate lit green.

She kept hold of my sleeve until the opening bars made her release me. I walked
beside her to the carriage door, but I did not touch it. She stepped aboard by
herself and took the nearest seat. I remained on the platform.

When the train moved, no shadows rose.

She watched me through the glass until the carriage entered the dark. The
warmth went with it. The gate closed before me, and when I laid my blank ticket
on the plate there was no light at all.

The station offered no thanks. Across the tracks, the hell board continued its
countdown for someone who had not yet appeared.

I returned to the bench. I sat at one end and laid the useless ticket on my
knee, leaving the place beside me clear.

The cold came up through the tiles. I stayed where I could be found.

stories.title: The Wrong Side of the Part
stories.prompt: You find a magical wig that, when worn, turns you into the exact oppose of who you are, with the wig changing to match the new personality. However, you don’t believe this… until you put it on.
stories.body:
# The Wrong Side of the Part

By three fifteen on the last day of the shop, I had made seventy-two decisions and none of them was the one that mattered.

SELL went on the acrylic heads and the hydraulic styling chair. DONATE went on three boxes of synthetic bobs that had survived two decades of fashion by never having participated in it. DISCARD went on dried adhesive, moth-nibbled switches, and a practice head whose remaining hair gave it the expression of a betrayed turnip.

I printed the labels in twelve-point type, centered. Grief was no excuse for crooked stationery.

The unsigned purchase contract lay beneath the appointment ledger, where I had put it while searching for a cloth to polish the mirrors. The mirrors did not need polishing. They were already honest enough to show the stripped shelves, pale rectangles on the walls, and me in my gray cardigan, reducing our mother's life's work to three verbs.

My phone vibrated.

**Four sharp,** Petra had written. **The buyer arrives at five. Please tell me we are still having a surprise-free afternoon.**

I typed, **Of course.**

Then, **Though I wondered if we might discuss—**

Then, **There are a few figures I don't quite—**

I deleted everything except **Of course**, added a smiling face so it wouldn't look hostile, and hated Petra for making me do it.

This was unfair, since Petra had not made me do anything. That was the useful feature of never saying what I wanted: other people could be guilty without the inconvenience of a trial.

Below her text sat a voice message from six months earlier. Seven minutes and twelve seconds. I had listened once, in the dark, after our mother was asleep upstairs. I had never played it again. I did not need to. Petra's voice had worn a groove through me.

I turned the phone facedown and chose a new task.

Our mother's oldest travelling case had escaped the labels because its brass catches were jammed. I worked them loose with the flat end of a tail comb. The case smelled of old powder, canvas, and the faint animal warmth that human hair kept long after it belonged to no one. Inside rested a row of setting pins, a stained veil, and nothing worth saving.

The bottom sounded hollow when I knocked it.

Beneath a false panel lay a wig wrapped in yellowing tissue. It was an ash-brown bob, center-parted, blunt at the jaw. Good hair, hand-knotted, wasted on a style so obedient it seemed to apologize for occupying the box.

A card had been tucked beneath the crown.

*Wear it and meet the person you are not.*

*Heat wakes it.*

*To take it off, tell the truth neither of you wants.*

I read it twice, which was one more time than it deserved.

Our mother had loved theatre without requiring a stage. She once told a nervous bride that the right hairpiece would frighten rain away, and it had not rained until after the photographs. This proved nothing except that weather occasionally cooperated with salesmanship.

“Magical wig,” I said to the empty shop. “Naturally. Very useful inventory note.”

Still, human-hair work had to be tried before it was donated. A warped foundation could pinch, and old elastic sometimes failed without warning. I could picture Petra asking whether I had checked it. I could picture myself saying no. The second image was less plausible.

I pinned up my own hair, loosened the adjustment tabs, and lowered the wig onto my head.

I did it voluntarily. I did it while disbelieving every word on the card. Later, those facts mattered to me, though they did not make what followed less mine.

The crown settled cool against my scalp. I slipped two fingers beneath the nape and tested the tension. The foundation was exquisite: fine lace, tiny knots, a spiral of denser work around the crown as deliberate as a fingerprint. Then my skin warmed it.

My next heartbeat struck the net like a plucked string.

Heat ran outward through the knots. Not heat arriving from the wig—mine, drawn from my scalp and pulse, distributed in bright little paths I could feel but not see. The lace contracted to my head. My attention caught on it, and the whole spiral seemed to fill with everything I knew I was: quiet, careful, accommodating, tidy. The list became a cage only because I supplied the bars.

The hair brushed my jaw.

Then it brushed my shoulders.

I grabbed the styling chair as the bob poured down and out. Ash brown deepened to copper-black, bright as a banked fire wherever the light struck. The center part slewed hard to the left and bleached bone-white in a line so straight it looked cut with a razor. Sleek lengths buckled into enormous coils. They crowded my shoulders, sprang halfway down my back, and tossed after every startled movement with the momentum of an entrance.

I stared into the salon mirror.

The woman in the glass stared back with my face and none of my apologies.

Nothing inside me went dark. I remembered the labels. I remembered the contract. I remembered why Petra wanted the sale and why I had said yes. I simply found all those reasons unbearably boring.

“Oh,” I said, and my voice came out rich with amusement. “There you are.”

I yanked off the gray cardigan and dropped it on the DISCARD pile.

The labels offended me next. Seventy-two tiny white surrender flags. I swept them from the counter, peeled SELL off the styling chair, slapped it onto the contract, and laughed so hard the copper-black coils bounced around my face.

My phone gave me the buyer's number from the email thread. I called.

“This is Tilda Bristow,” I said when a cautious voice answered. “A small correction to today's arrangements. The shop is not for sale.”

There was a silence filled with paper and alarm. “But the appointment—”

“Is an excellent opportunity for you to discover resilience.”

I ended the call.

Before I could lower the phone, Petra rang.

“I'm stuck at the lender,” she said. “The buyer asked for a corrected debt statement before the signing. Their system is down. I'll be there by quarter to five. Do not start without me.”

“Take your time,” I said, and heard how easily the new voice could make sabotage sound considerate.

Old me would have vomited from shame. I could remember that. I could even anticipate the practical consequences with perfect clarity: breach, delay, debt, Petra's fury. Yet relief fizzed through my blood. I had spent two years making grief presentable for other people. For once, I wanted witnesses to the mess.

The shop account was still signed in on my phone. I propped it against a canister of combs and recorded myself beneath the faded awning, framed by bare display hooks.

“At four thirty,” I told the lens, “we are holding a funeral for being agreeable. There will be free hair, poor judgment, and the public burial of a terrible property sale. Dress code: something you were told was too much.”

I posted it before prudence could crawl back into fashion.

Then I tore apart the sorting scheme. SELL, DONATE, and DISCARD fluttered together across the floor. I put a silver bouffant on the betrayed turnip and arranged the heads in the window like a jury of glamorous widows. I opened every box Petra had taped. Each rip of packing tape felt like taking a full breath after years in a tight collar.

People began arriving at four twenty-six.

There were only eight at first: nearby shopkeepers, former customers, two teenagers still in school clothes, and a man who claimed he had come because his partner had sent him for groceries. By four thirty-five there were perhaps fifteen, which was enough to fill the narrow shop and make disaster feel curated.

I became magnificent.

I fitted a violet crop onto a woman who had once returned a custom piece because her husband called it “attention-seeking.”

“He was right,” I told her, turning her toward the mirror. “Seek better attention.”

The room applauded.

I gave away a reserved lace-front to someone it had not been reserved for. I knew this was theft from tomorrow's obligations. I also knew exactly which drawer held the deposit slip. The knowledge did not stop my hands. That was the horror of it, hidden inside the champagne sparkle of being watched.

I modelled three pieces at once over the impossible coils and told the crowd which customers lied about cutting their own bangs. I described our most expensive stock as “mourning hair for rich people who expect grief to have a natural-looking hairline.” A few people looked offended; more bought things. The shop account's viewer count climbed.

Every suppressed observation came out sharpened for entertainment. My jokes were accurate enough to draw blood and funny enough that the wounded laughed first.

At four forty-three, Petra Bristow pushed through the door.

She wore her good coat and carried a document folder against her ribs. Her gaze went from the crowd to the open boxes, to the wig on my head, to the SELL sticker across the contract I had pinned to the wall.

“Tilda,” she said. “What have you done?”

“Improved the closing party.”

“There wasn't supposed to be a closing party.”

“Then I've improved it infinitely.”

The crowd laughed. Petra did not. She was three years younger than I was, but exasperation had always made her look like the elder sister appointed by a stern committee.

She came behind the counter and lowered her voice. “The buyer sent me your video.”

“Then we saved on invitations.”

“Take it down. Call back. Say you're ill.”

“At last, a diagnosis for owning an opinion.”

“This isn't an opinion. It's a jointly owned building under debt, and you just announced to the neighborhood that you can make unilateral decisions about it.”

The delight in me sharpened. She had found the point that hurt and mistaken it for a warning.

I climbed onto the low fitting platform. The coils rose and settled around me, too large for modesty. “Petra would like everyone to know the shop is jointly owned. This is legally true. It was jointly inherited. It was not jointly kept open. It was not jointly cleaned at midnight, or stocked, or defended to creditors. And when our mother got sick, she was not jointly lifted from bed or washed or persuaded to eat.”

The room changed temperature.

“Stop,” Petra said.

For years I had wanted her to say I was right. Wearing the wig, I wanted something sweeter: I wanted her unable to survive my rightness.

Petra looked at the people crowded between the wig stands. “Could everyone please leave?”

“No,” I said. “They came for the funeral.”

Her mouth tightened. “You told me you could manage. Every time I offered to come, you told me not to disrupt my life. You made every decision, Tilda, and then presented me with the invoice in a language I was supposed to guess.”

It landed because it was true.

Truth did not make me gentler. It made me reach for a larger weapon.

I picked up my phone. The old voice message waited in the thread, still seven minutes and twelve seconds, still private.

Petra saw the screen. Her face emptied.

“Don't.”

Ordinarily, that one word would have stopped me. I knew it should stop me now. I remembered sitting in the dark while her recorded voice broke, remembered deciding I would never use her confession against her. The promise was present in my mind, intact.

I pressed play.

Petra's voice filled the shop.

*I couldn't come back because every time I saw her like that, I was terrified. You made it look as if I was busy, and I let you, because cowardice sounded worse. I knew you were drowning. I knew, and I still—*

Petra knocked the phone from my hand. It skidded beneath the styling chair. The message kept playing.

No one laughed.

She crouched, but I was faster. I snatched up the phone, clipped the ugliest thirty seconds, and posted them with one line about the co-owner who had inherited half the shop and none of the sickroom.

The act took six taps.

Petra stared at me as if six taps were a distance she could not cross.

“The wig didn't invent that cruelty,” she said. “It just made you enjoy using it.”

My screen lit with a new email before I could answer.

The buyer had withdrawn the offer.

There it was: the thing I had wanted. The five-o'clock signature evaporated. The shop remained ours, along with its debt, its emptied shelves, and the echo of Petra's voice dying in the sudden quiet.

Petra picked up her folder.

“You wanted me punished,” she said. “You were just too polite to ask.”

Then she left.

The crowd followed in embarrassed pieces. One person set a free wig back on the counter. Another avoided my eyes while continuing to record. Within minutes I stood alone among ripped boxes and overturned categories.

The copper-black mass in the mirror was glorious. Its white part divided my head like a verdict.

I opened a live broadcast.

The shop account still had hundreds of viewers. Reactions climbed the screen: flames, question marks, hearts, demands for context. I angled the phone so the empty shop stretched behind me like conquered territory.

“Since everyone is suddenly interested in inheritance,” I began, “let's discuss who morally owns this place.”

I knew Petra owned half. I knew care could not transmute signatures. I knew I had hidden my resentment inside obedience, then called the hiding generosity. None of that knowledge had vanished. It merely stood at a distance while self-interest wore my skin beautifully.

My thumb hovered over the button that would send me live.

I wanted to press it.

I wanted the shop. I wanted the watching faces. I wanted Petra to hurt enough that my hurt would finally look proportionate. And beneath all of it, humiliating in its smallness, I wanted my sister to have noticed without being told.

At my temples, the crown pulsed.

Craft lived in my fingers deeper than temperament. I slid them beneath the coils and felt the lace. Each beat of my heart sent warmth along the radiating knots. The foundation was not a mind wrestling me. It was a focus, exquisitely worked and utterly inert without the living pattern I kept feeding it: meek against monstrous, silence against spectacle, one self defined by the rejection of the other.

The card had not said which truth, only that neither of us wanted it. There was no *us*. There were two postures I had used to avoid the same naked sentence.

I ended the broadcast before it began.

The empty shop offered no applause.

“I want the shop,” I said, “and I wanted Petra to know without ever making myself ask.”

The sentence hurt more than any accusation. It blamed no one. It guaranteed nothing. It made my desire visible where it could be refused.

The white part blurred.

Heat drained from the spiral of knots. The huge coils lost their spring and collapsed against my shoulders, copper-black fading through brown. The crown slackened under my fingers. I lifted the wig free.

By the time it reached the counter, it was the same drab, symmetrical bob I had taken from the case.

My gray cardigan waited on the rubbish pile.

I put it on, then took it off again.

Deleting the post did not delete the copies. A clipped version already had more views than the shop account had followers. The buyer's withdrawal remained politely final. Three messages demanded refunds for things I had given away. One asked whether the funeral would continue tomorrow.

I typed a public statement that said the disclosure had been mine, made without Petra's consent, and that no circumstance excused it. I did not mention the wig. “Magical hair made me do it” had the structure of a joke and the ethics of a trapdoor.

Then I sent Petra a message.

**I removed it. What I did is still mine. I am sorry I played and posted your message. I won't ask you to forgive me. Please come back only if you want to watch me make sure it cannot happen again. After that, I want to propose a fair process for the shop. You can say no.**

She did not answer.

At five twenty, she returned.

She stayed inside the locked door, coat still buttoned, while I set the ash-brown wig on a canvas block at the workbench. I turned the styling chair away from the mirror. For once I did not want to see myself as a client whose discomfort could be managed.

“Is that it?” Petra asked.

“Yes.”

“Can it do it again?”

“If someone wears it and supplies what it needs, I think so.”

“You think.”

“I only know what it did with me.”

I showed her the spiral construction at the crown: the tiny central knot from which the tension spread, the pathways that had carried my heat and pulse. Then, with a blunt needle and tweezers, I began to unwork it.

The first knot resisted because it was old and fine, not because it wished to remain. I teased it apart. Hair loosened across the block. I took out the next, then the next, destroying in minutes the skill of hands I would never identify.

Petra watched until the foundation opened and the wig became ordinary loose hair sliding onto the worktable.

“I'm sorry,” I said again. “The grievance was real. The cruelty was a choice I made while cruelty felt good. Both are true.”

“That doesn't fix it.”

“No.”

“People heard me.”

“Yes.”

“I don't know if I can forgive you.”

My old instinct rose at once: reassure her, release her, punish myself so thoroughly she would have to comfort me. I let the instinct pass without obeying it.

“You don't have to decide that today,” I said.

I put the loose hair in the DISCARD box. Then I peeled the label off.

On a fresh label I wrote DECIDE TOGETHER and stuck it over the torn cardboard.

Petra gave it a tired, suspicious look. “Stationery. Bold.”

“I'm starting within my range.”

Her mouth moved, almost a smile and not forgiveness.

I took the unsigned sale contract from the wall. On its blank back, I wrote what I should have written before the first box was packed: a formal accounting of the shop's debt, both our ownership, and the care work I had performed; an independent appraisal; thirty days for me to seek financing to buy Petra's share at a fair value; a sale after that if I could not. I added that I would make every possible correction to the public harm without repeating her private words.

“I will agree to the accounting and the appraisal,” Petra said. “That's all I'm agreeing to.”

“All right.”

“I am not agreeing to thirty days.”

“All right.”

“And I am not agreeing to save this place because you finally admitted you want it.”

The shop around us looked smaller without the wigs: just scuffed floorboards, shelves, two sisters, and a future that had declined to label itself.

“All right,” I said.

Then I read her the rest of my terms aloud.

stories.title: The City of Eleven Foundations
stories.prompt: There is a city that is architecturally colorful. It is divided by districts, and each district has its own style, like Gothic, Chinese, Egyptian, Greek, steampunk, cyberpunk, biopunk, dieselpunk, raypunk, solarpunk, and more. Notes: The story should focus on the city architecturally not the people or culture;
stories.body:
# The City of Eleven Foundations

The rain reached the receiving cisterns as dust.

For weeks, heat had bleached the solarpunk terrace's white ceramic walks and tightened the soil beneath its planted roofs. The linked reservoirs stood low enough for bottom floats to show through gauge glass. The terrace sat below the biopunk filter outlet and above the river works. First drops ticked on photovoltaic-blue canopies. Leaves and pale gravel detained those beads, but the cloud over the basin had turned noon light the color of slate.

Across the basin, eleven districts descended in wedges toward a river. Color sharpened wherever one foundation met another. Warm gold stopped at pearl enamel. Sea-glass teal ended against soot-black steel. Oxide red faced verdigris copper across a service alley. Ochre sandstone met pale limestone along a joint too narrow to hold a fallen coin. Blue-violet roofs crowded close to green and amber glazed tile without sharing a gutter. At the low center, board-marked concrete carried red, yellow, and cobalt bands down broad ramps to flood doors that had not opened in years.

Water began to disclose what color concealed.

Higher on another wedge, it ran onto layered eaves, then down chains into dry plinth channels beneath vermilion timber columns. The halls there stood above linked courtyards on dressed stone. Their mortise-and-tenon frames bore weight through dense sets of interlocking brackets under the eaves; their lower screens rested in grooves from which they could be lifted. Runoff crossed the first court, dropped a shallow step, and vanished into a radial drain.

On the basin's high shoulder, rain darkened old silt stripes in Egyptian settling basins. The steps rose between battered sandstone walls whose inward slopes thickened toward their foundations. Empty water marks showed how grit had once descended from terrace to terrace before reaching the lapis-and-turquoise channels below. A second radial drain carried the new brown trickle beneath them.

Below those basins, rain glossed Greek stoas, following their slight fall. Blue-green channels ended behind stylobate plugs. Beyond, Gothic gargoyles fed grilles over deep cisterns beneath colored glass. At the marked working level, a low throat crossed each downhill wall into a dry masonry channel ending above the biopunk beds. Flying buttresses stepped across gravel-footed lanes.

Elsewhere the storm struck newer surfaces harder. It drummed on copper boiler courts, flowed past brass gauges, and pattered through pipe galleries above reciprocating lift pumps. Their intake descended to the central undercroft; their discharge ended at the high Egyptian basins. Rain slicked the painted-over teeth of a disused coupling where the copper district touched the steel sheds below. Beyond that joint, an elevated compression engine turned a black flywheel, driving a discharge pump nearer the river.

Rain made cyan and magenta pressure strips shine against matte composite walls. Those passive bands followed sealed utility conduits into the cyberpunk foundation, then disappeared under a district of grown cellulose ribs and leaf-green membranes. There, root rafts filled cavities between soil and structure. Dry reed galleries and cream-colored fungal beds waited above the ordinary watercourse, their outlet lip sloping toward the solarpunk cistern mouths below. Moisture thickened the outer fibers of the roots, as moisture always did.

A pneumatic carrier passed through a raypunk freight tube with a diminishing rush. The lower shutters clapped closed behind it. High above pearl canopies, pressure-balancing shafts exhaled through amber fins. At the center, the brutalist court remained almost dry beneath its coffered roof. Its undercroft lay empty behind flood doors, a low gray volume held between shear walls and caissons driven deeper than the foundations around it.

Beneath all eleven districts, the radial drains entered one service ring. At each border, a high-water float actuated a linkage that dropped a bulkhead closed; the gate had to lift to reopen. The bulkheads had protected foundations from small backflows, pipe fires, and neighboring spills. On maintenance plates beside them, worn tool arcs ended at cleanly painted boundary lines.

Then the cloudburst covered both the city and the short valley upstream. The separate trickles became eleven loads delivered to the same buried ring.

* * *

At the river, branches came down broadside in the surge. They tangled against the dieselpunk outfall screen, caught roof grit, reeds, and a rolling burden of silt, and flattened into a dense mat. The check gate swung inward against its stop.

It had closed correctly. That correctness sealed the only low exit from the city.

The discharge pump pulled against the blocked mouth. Its housing shook, first with a full mechanical beat and then with the dry rattle of cavities forming where water should have filled the impeller. The outlet gauge stopped rising. Above it, the engine continued to drive the flywheel while no water passed the shut gate.

Rain still entered from every slope.

In the buried service ring, the first high-water float rose until its linkage dropped a sector bulkhead. Iron met its sill with a concussion carried through concrete. Backflow stopped at that border. The next pulse, denied the volume beyond, climbed higher in the adjoining compartment. A second float rose. Another gate fell. Closures traveled around the basin—not together, but according to eleven different rates of runoff.

The ring lost its equal waterline. It became a necklace of sealed chambers, some holding air above a rising surface, some already running full. Every incoming drain added height to one compartment and force against the gates on either side.

In the cyberpunk wedge, cyan pressure strips brightened beside the sealed service floors. Magenta followed, lengthening upward along the utility risers as pressure bowed membranes behind them. The light came from compression changing the strips’ physical response; it interpreted nothing. Yet it made the hidden condition plain. The outfall gauge at the river remained fixed while, farther and farther uphill, colored bands showed a head of water still rising.

The first boundary had been protected. The shared foundation had been divided into eleven pressure vessels.

* * *

The matte composite foundation absorbed almost nothing. Waterproof faces turned the trapped surge sideways until it found the annular gap around a utility sleeve. Water knifed through that small opening and entered the softer ground beneath the biopunk district.

The root rafts were built to spread ordinary rain. They took water into layered fibers, thickened, and pressed more firmly into the soil that supported the grown ribs above. In a season of measured flow, that swelling closed erosion paths. Under the sudden buried surge, it narrowed the only remaining throat. Fine roots packed against the utility sleeve. The water behind them rose faster.

One cyan strip became solid light. A magenta length reached the underside of a cantilevered block.

Pressure worked past the root mass through gravel seams and struck the Egyptian foundation broadside. The battered walls carried the lateral push into their thicker bases. The stone yielded so little that the force changed direction. Muddy water spread along the base, searching, until it found the prepared sand and rubble beneath the neighboring Greek stylobate.

The first effect in the Greek court was dry.

A thread of white dust spilled from the edge of one column base. The open rills held only rainwater, but the saturated bed below had begun to lose its even bearing. Pressure raised one end of a paving slab by the thickness of a leaf. The next slab stayed down. Along the stoa, a line of pale columns that had been straight enough to vanish in perspective now showed one broken interval.

Another bulkhead fell beneath the central court.

The closure sent a blunt pulse backward. Greek drain plugs shivered in their sockets. The Egyptian mass held, the swollen roots tightened, and the sealed composite walls admitted nothing. Each sound foundation passed the excess to a joint less able to refuse it.

The shifted column remained standing. Its misalignment was nevertheless the first wound the storm wrote above ground, in a court whose own floor was scarcely wet.

* * *

The next pulse crossed beneath the Greek compartment and tore gravel from around the nearest Gothic buttress feet. The narrow lanes filled at their edges as gargoyles poured through the rain. Below the grilles, the vaulted cisterns still had room; the closed sector gate kept the foundation pressure from reaching them. They could accept falling water from roofs but not the trapped water lifting from beneath.

One buttress settled outward. The stone moved less than a finger’s width, but the movement altered the lateral thrust it had been built to carry. Inside the tall hall, a blue pane threw its reflection at an angle across the black floor. Violet light narrowed along one rib and widened along the next.

At the Chinese-derived halls, the same ground movement traveled differently. One stone plinth dipped as fines washed from beneath it. A vermilion column descended with the plinth; its tenoned beam shifted within the joint instead of splitting, and the layered dougong above redistributed the small change beneath the wide eave. Green glazed tiles chattered, settled, and held their overlapping courses.

The timber frame had room to accommodate motion. The soil did not. Brown water appeared at the lower edge of a dry plinth channel and carried pale grains into the stepped courtyard. A screen bowed where its sill no longer sat level. The primary columns remained vertical enough to bear, while the foundation continued to lose material.

Across the basin, capacities stood isolated from the loads they might have relieved. Water entered the steampunk boiler court above the hubs. It hissed against iron doors, drowned the lower fireboxes, and quenched the pressure that should have powered the reciprocating pumps. Their rods stopped at uneven heights. Brass gauge needles sank.

The diesel engine remained dry on its elevated frame. It could supply torque, but its shaft still drove the useless discharge pump at the blocked outfall. Between the two districts, the old coupling teeth were hidden under several skins of green and red paint.

In the raypunk district, compressed air had nowhere to go. Water entered the lower ring while the freight-tube shutters remained closed above it. Each rising pulse squeezed a pocket of air into a shorter length. When the pocket rebounded, the shock struck pipe brackets and bulkhead faces. Glass-block towers trembled in their mortar. High pressure shafts, built to vent the freight system, stood cut off from the ring by those lower shutters.

The central undercroft remained empty. Its flood doors divided the rising ring from enough gray volume to blunt the peak, but their locking pins were still seated. Along the descending surface route, the solarpunk cistern gauges still showed unused depth above the river works. Rain collected slowly in planted terraces, detained among stems and gravel, while the low city filled faster beneath the ground.

Occupation withdrew along the slope. Lifts stopped with their cars above the lowest landings. Fire doors stood propped along upward routes. Laundry lines emptied; carts and benches disappeared from courts; loose screens were taken from the paths of water. Window light went dark first beside the river, then in climbing rows. Chalk marks appeared above wet thresholds. Tool chests stood open at service hatches, their contents no longer arranged.

No crowd remained in the architecture’s lowest rooms, but evacuation changed no load below them.

At three places, the danger was visible. Colored glass remained skewed above the scoured Gothic footing. The Greek column line broke the eye at its displaced base. Under the brutalist court, cobalt and yellow paving bands rose in a shallow ridge over the crown of the service ring.

The ridge climbed with the next hammer stroke.

* * *

Keeping the sector gates closed would preserve dry galleries, polished floors, and the empty central undercroft for a little longer. It would also keep every rising compartment narrow enough to tear at its neighbors. If the ring crown split, pressurized water would scour outward below all eleven foundations, beyond the reach of any open court or settling stair.

The alternative could be read in the city’s levels.

The undercroft lay below the ring crown behind doors designed to flood. Raypunk shafts rose above every expected waterline. The diesel flywheel aligned with the steampunk pump shafts. Egyptian basins received the route's only lifted water. Greek floors fell into Gothic cisterns and Chinese-derived courtyards along separate branches. Below their reunion, the biopunk outlet stood above the solarpunk receiving cisterns; both remained above the river works. The reservoirs had capacity because their terraces were still delaying the rain.

The route existed, but only as disconnected fragments. Connecting it would put river mud into the central undercroft, silt onto ochre stone, water across white plaster, a dark line on basalt, and pressure against timber screens. It would load reeds and fungi with every fine particle the settling steps missed. It would exchange the possibility of pristine interiors for certain damage.

The first changed object was a broken warning seal beside the brutalist flood doors.

Locking pins came out of their sockets and appeared stacked on a ramp above the rising ridge. A wet wrench lay across a gate housing. Lower freight shutters stood open beneath the raypunk tubes, their release handles left down. The painted skins over the border coupling had been cut away, exposing toothed steel. At the Greek stoas, stylobate plugs rested on folded cloth. Gothic cistern grilles leaned against walls. The lowest timber screens had been lifted from their grooves where they could be saved; others, already bound by the shifted plinths, remained in place. Spill panels between the stepped courts stood propped open.

These were not automatic responses. The floats had closed the gates. The new arrangement bore the marks of tools and many passages through the rain.

The cobalt ridge rose again. A paving joint opened and released a thin line of brown foam.

Then the central flood doors swung inward, and the first sector bulkhead began to lift.

* * *

The brutalist undercroft took the released surge.

Water struck its back wall hard enough to climb the board marks, then spread across the broad floor. The empty volume converted height into width. Shear walls received the first lateral blow; deep caissons carried the shifting load below the softened surface layers. Mud covered the lowest red wayfinding band. A maintenance cabinet tore loose and lodged against a ramp, but the ring crown stopped rising.

The release also drove trapped air ahead of it. With the lower raypunk shutters open, compressed air entered the freight tubes and climbed the pressure-balancing shafts. Glass blocks fogged from within. Air burst above the flood line through amber fins, shaking rain from the parabolic canopies. One last hammer stroke rang through the lower brackets. Then the pockets had an upward path, and the following pressure arrived as a long push rather than a blow.

At the industrial border, the diesel engine changed work. The shaft to the blocked discharge pump had been disengaged; oily teeth stood motionless over the jammed outfall line. Across the service alley, the exposed coupling joined the black flywheel to the steampunk transmission. There was no elegance in the fit. Old tooth faces struck, slipped, caught, and shed flakes of paint. Dark iron rods began moving in the flooded copper pump house.

The reciprocating lift pumps drew mud-heavy water from the buffered undercroft. With every stroke, valves opened and shut in physical sequence. The dry engine labored under the added load. Its orange flywheel mark slowed enough to become a succession of arcs. In the copper district, drowned boilers stayed cold while pump rods rose under borrowed torque.

The pumps' sole lifted discharge reached the high Egyptian basins with the force of a broken gutter. It hit the upper step, threw brown water against turquoise faience, and spread between the battered walls. Those walls took the new lateral load through their thickened bases. At each drop, the current broadened and slowed. Branch grit accumulated first; coarse sand followed in crescent bars. The water crossing the lowest ochre lip remained cloudy, but it no longer carried stones large enough to scar a pump valve or jam an open rill.

Pressure strips still burned solid in three cyberpunk service levels. Rain continued entering the ring faster than the first pump strokes lifted it. In the brutalist undercroft, mud reached the yellow band.

From that high settling head, clarified overflow descended across the Greek border. The removed stylobate plugs had exposed the ends of two channels. Water entered the subtle grades of the stoas and divided, half curving toward the Gothic lanes, half toward the timber-framed courtyards. The split reduced the thrust on the already displaced paving. White plaster darkened along both rills. At the shifted column, water passed on either side instead of striking the weakened base. Its broken perspective did not worsen.

The first branch descended through the Gothic gargoyle channels and poured through open grilles into deep cisterns. Vaulted chambers stored the leading surge, transferring its weight rib by rib into piers. Basalt lower courses acquired a black-brown tide line. As the water rose, pressure beneath the scoured buttress compartment fell. At the marked working level, the branch entered the low throat in the downhill wall, passed through a falling masonry channel, and emerged above the biopunk beds. The blue pane’s reflection crept closer to its old angle.

The second branch crossed raised stone plinths through the opened channels of the Chinese-derived district. It dropped from one courtyard to the next under deep layered eaves. The flow found a lower screen trapped in its warped groove, bowed the lattice, and broke it free. Timber fragments traveled only as far as the next stone sill. Above, mortise-and-tenon joints admitted small rotations without surrendering the beam ends, while dougong sets spread altered roof loads across adjacent columns. Water stained the plinths. Green and amber tiles continued shedding new rain into the same controlled path. The frame kept its primary geometry while accepting the loss of what had been made to yield first.

At the beds, Gothic masonry outflow met the Chinese-derived courtyard branch. Reed stems bent flat under the initial flow and rose partway when it passed. Root mats that had constricted the buried surge now held the opened soil along the surface route. Water spread through cream fungal layers and permeable membranes. Fine silt lodged among fibers; the beds darkened from leaf green to wet umber. Their pores narrowed as material accumulated. The lift pumps had to slow, or the water would overtop them before filtration could occur.

The diesel flywheel lost another measure of speed. Mud climbed above the yellow band in the central undercroft. Along the cyberpunk foundations, magenta pressure remained high beside two sealed utility sleeves. The whole sequence balanced on rates that no single district could absorb.

But the raypunk shafts continued venting, so the slower strokes did not trap another hammer. The undercroft continued spreading each pulse. Grit kept settling on the Egyptian stairs. The two Greek grades kept flow away from the shifted column. The Gothic vaults and stepped timber courts gave the filters time by storing and stretching their branches.

At last, water emerged from the biopunk beds with only a pale haze. It crossed the outlet lip and descended through open receiving lines. The first solarpunk cistern received it below its lowest gauge mark. Linked reservoirs passed the rise from one white ceramic chamber to the next. Overhead, planted terraces were only then beginning to release their detained roof water. Their delay left room for the filtered flood descending from above.

One cyan pressure strip shortened by the width of a slab.

Then another did.

Sector by sector, the buried head fell. Magenta retreated from the cantilevered service floors. Waterlines met across the raised bulkheads instead of battering them from opposite heights. In the brutalist court, the brown foam at the lifted paving joint thinned and stopped. The ring crown held beneath the ridge.

The Gothic buttress did not return to its former bed, but it ceased moving. Colored light steadied on the wet floor. The Greek column stayed fractionally out of line, fixed now against a level that no longer changed. Through the timber halls, the chatter of glazed tile became only the sound of rain.

On the receiving terrace, cistern gauges rose into their clear tubes.

* * *

The river took longer to fall than the rain. When its surface finally dropped below the outlet mouth, the check gate eased from its stop. The branch-and-silt mat remained packed over the screen, now reachable from the bank but not yet cleared. Nothing about that delayed repair had saved the city. Survival already showed in the route of the mud.

It striped the brutalist undercroft to the height of the yellow band. It filled corners behind the shear walls and dried in the board marks. The Egyptian basins held bars of grit on every step. White stoa floors carried brown edges. Gothic basalt kept a tide line below the colored glass. Several timber screens were missing, and one stone plinth waited above a void to be packed and pinned. The biopunk reed beds lay bent beneath the silt they had caught. Their living fibers would grow or fail according to ordinary light, water, and repair; the clogged sections were cut out and replanted.

Repairs did not erase the storm’s diagram. The Greek column base was reset, but a narrow bronze line marked its displaced position. New grilles over the Gothic cisterns could be lifted without breaking paving. The courtyard spill panels were rehung above fresh stone channels. At the industrial border, the coupling remained bare and accessible under a jointed cover instead of paint. The raypunk shutters acquired external release bars. In the service ring, bulkheads were reset to rest raised over low equalization slots until high-water floats actuated and dropped them closed.

Most visible were the seams across the borders. Narrow spillways interrupted colored bands without smearing them together. Cobalt concrete still met sea-glass enamel cleanly. Ochre stone still ended at pale limestone. Vermilion timber still rose above its own gray plinths, distinct from the black basalt beyond. Only the routes for shared pressure crossed.

Shutters reopened downslope. Ventilation stirred damp curtains behind windows. Lift rails shone with new oil. Fresh footprints passed through the drying Greek court, vanished on dark stone, and appeared again as mud on a repaired plinth. Warm squares of light returned to the basin after sunset.

At one boundary, a thread of rain descended a green glazed tile, entered a newly cut channel in the raised stone, and crossed through a bronze-lined joint into the pale rill beside it. A small wet footprint overlaid the seam. The water kept both colors in its reflection as it moved on.

stories.title: The Shape of Mercy
stories.prompt: You are a child of a great mage lineage, your eldest sister could turn forests into ash with her flames, your older brother capable of freezing oceans over, your younger sibling, a tamer of magical beasts, but for some reason, everyone fears you the most, and you have zero clue why.
stories.body:
# The Shape of Mercy

Evelyn Bellweather, my eldest sister, could turn forests to ash. She had once stopped a wildfire by burning the untouched trees ahead of it. The songs omitted the black hills, the displaced villages, and the scars beneath her left glove. Marcus Bellweather, my older brother, had frozen an ocean reach hard enough to march an army across it, although he maintained that the fish had been deeply impressed. Phoebe Bellweather, my younger sibling, could put her hand against the muzzle of a raging magical beast and feel where terror ended and hunger began.

I could make a supper knife nervous.

"It's steel," Marcus murmured beside me. "If you glare any harder, it may discover an ancestral gift."

"Perhaps it will appoint me its steward."

He smiled, but his hand went still around his warded cup.

At the head of the table, Lady Rowena Bellweather rose. Candlelight caught the silver stitched through her dark sleeves: little channels for the living wards she supplied with every breath. Beyond the tall windows, the orchard pressed green and restless against the glass. Its trees had been cultivated by generations of the family to flower in every season. Tonight, white petals clung to the panes like curious moths.

Relations, household officers, and tenants filled the long tables. They had come to hear the succession appointments, particularly mine. House Bellweather held that a child's magic followed the shape of an early, ruling desire. Evelyn had wanted warmth. Marcus had wanted stillness. Phoebe had wanted to know why a trapped fox screamed when nobody touched it.

According to my mother, I had wanted nothing remarkable.

I had accepted that. Mostly. The appointment would make usefulness official even if magic never did.

"A great house is not sustained by power alone," Rowena began.

One of the clerks had laid out the household ledger near her elbow. Its brown leather and cheap black ink looked shabby among the warded crystal. Earlier, when I suggested that every appointment be entered twice and witnessed, my mother had said, not unkindly, "Ink is for people whose word cannot defend itself."

Now she rested two fingers on the page. "Adrian Bellweather will serve as—"

The orchard doors exploded inward.

Wind crossed the hall like a thrown table. Candles vanished. Platters skated. My unwarded cup struck the wall and survived, which I thought showed character.

Something vast shouldered through the wreckage.

It stood taller than a carriage horse, though no horse had antlers branching like a winter tree or stormlight moving under translucent skin. Blood darkened an old scar around its throat. Each breath dragged the smell of rain and hot iron into the room. Lightning crawled from tine to tine above its lowered head.

Phoebe rose so quickly that her chair toppled. "Don't strike it."

Behind the stormhart came Garran Bellweather.

My father had been gone ten years. I remembered him as a broad, laughing man who could make hounds sit with a crooked finger and courtiers confess with a hand on their shoulder. The man in the doorway was leaner. His formal coat shone with rain, and a dull metal bracelet circled one wrist.

Every member of my family looked at me.

Not at Evelyn, whose fingers had already begun to glow. Not at Marcus, around whose boots frost feathered the floor. At me.

Garran followed their gaze and laughed without pleasure.

"There you are," he said. "Put back what you took."

I had imagined several versions of my father's return. In none of them did he bring an indoor thunderstorm or accuse me of theft before the soup was cleared.

"You will leave," my mother said.

The silver channels in her sleeves flared. Wards rose across the broken doors in overlapping panes of blue light.

Garran lifted the bracelet. The stormhart's scar tightened as if an invisible hand had twisted it.

Phoebe gasped.

"Wait," she said. She had one palm extended, not touching the beast. Her face changed with every breath it took—fear, fury, confusion passing over her features like clouds. "There are two wants in it."

"Move away, Phoebe," Evelyn said.

"The storm is its own. The fear is its own." Phoebe swallowed. "But something under them keeps saying forward. Kill. It isn't listening to him. It's trapped in something he already made."

My father had created command-bonds once. I knew that much. His magic had been the family embarrassment, though nobody had ever explained why a talent praised in war had become unspeakable at home.

The bracelet clicked against his wrist. It was only a focus, but the old command still lived where the scar crossed the stormhart's living flesh, drawing strength from the heart it tormented.

"I cannot make another bond," Garran said. "Your precious Adrian saw to that. But this one remembers its master."

The stormhart hurled itself against Rowena's wards.

The first pane burst. My mother staggered.

Guests fled between the tables. A second impact cracked every window on the orchard side. Phoebe cried out in the same instant as the beast, clutching her throat.

"Adrian can stop it," Garran said. "Can't you, son?"

"I don't know what you're talking about."

Something almost gentle entered his expression. "No. Of course you don't."

The stormhart charged.

Evelyn moved first. She struck both hands toward the orchard, and ashfire poured through the shattered doors in a white-orange sheet. It did not touch the fleeing people. It raced past them, choosing grass and leaf, carving a crescent of bare earth between the Hall and the oldest trees.

The orchard screamed.

Not in words. In sap bursting to steam, in branches snapping, in the rush of birds abandoning nests. The nearest rows became black shapes against a furnace glow. Evelyn stood rigid at the center of it, directing destruction so it would remain rescue. Smoke leaked through the seams of her glove.

The stormhart veered from the heat. Its hooves struck the ornamental pond, and water erupted high enough to hammer the windows.

Marcus thrust out his hands.

Cold took the flood in midair.

For one impossible moment, a wave curved over us, clear as glass. Then it crashed down as ice. A wall of frozen water divided the stormhart from the guests already sheltering in the far gallery, penning them there but keeping the beast out. Frost raced across the pond, the courtyard stones, and the broken doors. It sealed three exits and locked the beast inside the crescent Evelyn had burned.

"Saved everyone," Marcus panted. "Minor issue with saving us."

Lightning struck the ice.

Blue fire split and multiplied through it. The Hall's remaining windows burst inward. Rowena's wards caught most of the shards, then went dark. Marcus was thrown against a pillar. He slid down, dazed, one sleeve glazed white where his own cold had turned against him.

The stormhart reared. Wind tore charred branches from the orchard and drove them through the room.

I crawled behind the overturned table. Phoebe lay a few feet away, curled on her side. Her eyes were open, but they did not see the Hall.

"It hurts," she whispered. "It can't stop wanting to run. It can't stop being ordered forward."

I caught her wrist.

The world opened.

Not visibly. The Hall remained smoke and ice and scattered silver. Yet beneath it I perceived connections with the certainty of fingers finding knots in darkness.

Phoebe's gift ran from her toward the stormhart in a trembling, open braid. Nothing hooked it at either end. She was not holding the beast. She was making room inside herself for its terror, and that generosity was drowning her.

The stormhart's lightning moved through its bones in branching silver currents, fierce and wholly its own.

Around the scar lay another connection: a hard black twist driven into living flesh, carrying one command in endless circles. Forward. Kill. Forward. Its far end passed not into Garran's body but through the bracelet he used to pull the bond taut. The metal shaped an intention made a decade ago. It supplied none of its own.

Beyond them I felt Evelyn's ashfire, red and ravenous, joined to the living core of her as intimately as breath. Marcus's cold was a deep blue pressure folded behind his heart. My mother's wards threaded from pulse to silver to stone.

Every connection presented an edge.

And in me, some old desire lifted its head.

Stop.

I released Phoebe and the perception remained.

Evelyn saw my face. Her flame faltered.

Not surprise. Recognition.

"What am I?" I asked.

Garran smiled. "At last."

Another bolt struck Marcus's ice. Cracks flashed beneath our knees.

"Tell him," Marcus said.

My mother rounded on him. "Not now."

"We ran out of later ten years ago."

Evelyn lowered one burning hand, though the firebreak continued to blaze. "When you were nine, father tried to bind Phoebe."

My memory offered fragments before she could give me any. Phoebe at six, sobbing in the old beast room. My father's hand around her small wrist. A fox in a cage clawing its paws bloody while Phoebe begged it to bite her instead of obeying him.

Then morning.

I remembered morning with unnatural clarity: Marcus sitting beside my bed with both hands tucked beneath his arms; Evelyn's left glove burned through at the palm; my mother saying my father had gone away and that I had been ill. Between the beast room and the bed lay one clean, impossible absence.

"He said her affinity could command anything alive if he trained it properly," Evelyn continued. "She kept telling him that wasn't what she did. He made her feel the fox's pain until she complied."

"I was forging a weapon no enemy could resist," Garran said. "For this family."

Phoebe lifted her head. "You were teaching me that love and obedience were the same."

The stormhart shuddered with her. Its antlers scraped lightning across the ceiling.

Marcus pushed himself upright against the pillar. "You ran at him, Adrian. You grabbed his arm. Then every command-bond in the room fell apart."

"Not only the bonds," Evelyn said. "His gift. All of it."

Garran spread his empty hands. "I woke inside a dead world. Every living will I had once felt was gone. Even the smallest thread. Your brother made me harmless."

The word landed like a challenge.

"I don't remember."

"That is your gift's price," Rowena said.

My mother looked older than she had at the head of the table. Without her bright wards, her sleeves were only cloth and metal.

"Bellweather power takes the shape of desire," she said. "Yours answered the desire to make something stop. You sever magical connections. When the cut is complete, your mind loses its memory of making that cut. Not your childhood. Not your knowledge or your love. The act itself, and the moments in which you perform it. A mirrored absence."

"How do you know?"

Her mouth tightened.

"Because we tested you," Evelyn said. Shame roughened her voice. "Small spells. You agreed each time—but only after each cut had begun. The question, the answer, the completion: all of it fell inside the absence. Then mother stopped. She destroyed the notes."

"I protected you," Rowena said.

"From what?"

No one answered quickly enough.

I looked from Evelyn's rigid shoulders to Marcus's careful hands, to the plain square beneath my chair.

"You protected yourselves."

"Both," my mother said. At least she did not soften it. "I knew what fear would make others do to you. And I knew what you could do to us if you understood."

The last ten years rearranged themselves. Evelyn stepping away whenever anger warmed her face. Marcus turning every accidental touch into a joke. My mother denying me lessons, duties, even warded cutlery. Phoebe alone reaching for me without calculation.

They had not pitied my emptiness. They had feared their own.

Garran pulled the bracelet again. The command bit deeper. Phoebe screamed, and the stormhart drove its antlers into the ice wall. Cracks spread toward the guests penned in the far gallery.

"You see them now," Garran said to me. "All their lovely weapons pointed at your throat. Take Evelyn's fire. Take Marcus's cold. Strip Rowena's wards. Give them the mercy they gave me: a life in which no one need fear them."

My mother stepped between us. "Adrian, do nothing."

There it was: my father's command and my mother's, dressed differently but each certain my choice belonged to them.

The edge inside me sharpened.

It would have been easy to obey the shape of my oldest desire. Stop the fire. Stop the ice. Stop the storm. Stop every power that had ever made a room tense when I entered it. The connections lay together before me, and fear blurred their boundaries.

Harmless, I understood, was merely what frightened people called someone they had successfully diminished.

Safe was harder.

I crawled to Phoebe through glass and slush. "Look at me."

Her pupils were storm-wide.

"I need to know what belongs to it," I said. "Not what would make this easier. What does it want?"

She pressed both hands to the floor. Her gift opened wider. Wind shook her hair loose, and for a moment her face held an anguish too large to be human.

"It wants the storm," she said. "The lightning. It wants to break the walls and run under open sky. That's all its. Adrian, don't take that."

"And the order?"

"Foreign. Old. It hurts every time it resists." She fixed on me. "Cut that. Only that."

The stormhart struck the ice again.

"Evelyn," I said, "lower the fire."

She looked toward the orchard. Beyond her firebreak, living branches smoked. If she released the ashfire too quickly, ordinary flame might leap the gap. If she held it, the beast would remain penned.

Then she closed her fist.

The white heart vanished from the flames. What remained sank into char and wet earth, dangerous but mortal. Evelyn pulled off her scorched glove and showed me her empty hand.

"Marcus. Let the ice go."

"It is keeping the antlers out of our relatives."

"And keeping the storm in."

He looked at the cracks, then at me. The joke he might have made never came.

Marcus lowered both palms. The abyssal pressure folded inward. Ice softened at its edges, water rushing through narrow channels instead of shattering at once. The guests fell back toward the gallery's inner doors as the barrier slumped away from them.

Their restraint separated the connections. Red withdrew. Blue receded. The stormhart's own silver blaze remained, and beneath it the black command stood stark as wire through a wound.

My mother seized my shoulder.

I felt her wards at once, every one of them vulnerable.

She let go as though burned.

"You will forget," she said.

"Yes."

The thought frightened me more than the storm. Choice was how we shaped ourselves. What did it mean to choose if I could not keep the choosing?

On the floor near the overturned head table lay the household ledger, its pages soaked at the edges but intact. The inkpot had rolled beneath a chair.

"Marcus," I said. "You wanted me to steward records. Start with mine."

He understood. He dragged himself to the ledger, found the pen, and tore out a blank appointment page. His fingers shook from cold and injury.

"No enchantment," I said.

"Cheapest ink in the house."

"Write this. I, Adrian Bellweather, being informed that severance will remove my memory of performing it, choose to cut the command forcing this stormhart to kill. I do not consent to cut its storm, Phoebe's bond, or any other gift."

Marcus wrote. Evelyn knelt and steadied the paper. Phoebe, still shaking, placed her hand beside theirs.

I signed beneath the words. The pen tore the wet paper after the last letter, but the name held.

"Witnessed," Marcus said.

"Witnessed," Evelyn and Phoebe answered.

My mother stared at the page as if cheap ink had overturned a throne.

Then she said, "Witnessed."

Garran lunged for the paper.

Rowena moved first. No spell—only her body. She caught his wrist and drove him to his knees against the flooded floor. The bracelet struck stone.

"You owe me," he snarled at me.

"I owe you the truth that what I did was irreversible and without your consent." I went to him, close enough to see rain caught in his lashes. "I was nine. You were hurting Phoebe. Both facts matter."

"Then restore me."

"I can't."

His face broke around the answer.

For one breath I saw not a monster, but a man who had lost a sense through another person's frightened hand and been left ten years with no account of his own undoing. The grief was real. It did not make the stormhart's pain less real.

"I will not cut you again," I said. "There is nothing in you I need to cut."

I turned to the beast.

Without Evelyn's ashfire, the stormhart advanced. Without Marcus's hard ice, it could choose its footing. Phoebe rose beside me, maintaining the open braid of her gift though blood ran from one nostril.

"I'm here," she told it. "The pain isn't the whole world."

Lightning crowned its antlers. Thunder struck inside my ribs.

I reached—not with my hands, though I held them out—and found the foreign command where it entered the scar. I traced it carefully past the beast's rage, past Phoebe's compassion, past the silver current of the storm. The black twist fought by tightening. It had one purpose, made long ago by a living will and kept alive by the creature it compelled.

Forward. Kill.

I found its edge.

The last thing I remembered was choosing how narrow mercy should be.

* * *

I woke the next morning with smoke in my hair and a missing piece of the night.

The gap began beside the stormhart. I remembered the command before me. I remembered Marcus bending over the ledger. I remembered choosing.

Then sunlight lay across my bed.

For a few minutes, I considered the attractive possibility that everyone else had been eaten and I could avoid the conversation. Then Phoebe opened the door without knocking.

Evelyn and Marcus followed. My mother came last, carrying the ledger page.

All four looked exhausted. Evelyn's bare hand was bandaged. Marcus leaned on the doorframe. Phoebe's eyes were swollen, but when I asked about the stormhart she smiled.

"It kept its lightning," she said. "It broke the last orchard wall and ran. I guided it until it no longer needed me."

"And Garran?"

"Confined in an unwarded room," my mother said. "The bracelet is locked away as evidence, not destroyed."

They told me what had happened after the edge.

The black command had come apart. The scar remained, but no intention moved through it. The stormhart had thrown its head back and released one bolt into the open sky, its own anger at last. Phoebe had led it through the melting ice. I had collapsed before it cleared the orchard.

Each account matched. Not perfectly—Marcus insisted my fall had possessed tragic dignity; Evelyn said I had folded like wet laundry—but in every part that mattered.

Then my mother handed me the paper.

My consent stood in Marcus's handwriting with my signature beneath it. Below were four witness signatures and, lower down, a second account written before dawn. The paper was buckled from water. The ink had bled around my name. It had never held a spark of magic.

It held.

"I called concealment mercy," my mother said. "It was fear made respectable."

"It was also love," I said.

Her eyes brightened.

"That does not make it honest."

I read the account twice. I could not make myself remember the act. Evidence did not fill the absence or return ownership in the simple way I wanted. But my choice had left a shape in the world: a living beast gone free with its storm intact, my siblings still themselves, a scar emptied of command.

"About the stewardship," Rowena began.

"I accept."

Marcus blinked. "You might at least bargain before surrendering."

"I have terms."

"There he is."

I held up the page.

"Every severance gets an unenchanted record, begun before the act when possible and completed by witnesses afterward. No testing me without informed consent. No concealment of my history, especially from me. I will not cut a person's gift without their consent except to stop immediate coercion or immediate harm, and even then I choose the narrowest connection I can."

"That is a great deal of authority to claim," my mother said.

"Then appoint someone harmless."

For a moment, nobody moved.

Evelyn crossed the room first. All my life, she had measured the distance between her anger and my skin. Now she sat on the bed and put her bandaged hand over mine.

"Agreed," she said.

Marcus laid his cold fingers over hers. "Agreed."

Phoebe climbed onto the other side of the bed and nearly crushed my foot. "Obviously agreed."

My mother looked at our joined hands. Fear had not left her face. I suspected it would live there for some time, as Garran's grief would live in the truth of what I had done to him.

Fear, at least, was honest enough to negotiate with.

Rowena added her hand.

"Agreed," she said.

Outside, the living orchard smoked in the morning sun. The burned crescent would take years to mend. Meltwater ran from Marcus's broken wall. Somewhere beyond it, thunder rolled farther away—not silenced, not tamed, only free to choose its direction.

I signed the stewardship appointment with the cheapest ink in Bellweather Hall.

stories.title: The Weight of Falling Up
stories.prompt: You're an apprentice at a prestigious magic school! It's time for you to take your flying assessment, and take to the skies. Others choose brooms, levitation spells, or mounts. You show up with something a little different.
stories.body:
# The Weight of Falling Up

By the time Examiner Dovek called my name, three people had already left the roof. Two had chosen brooms, which was what sensible people at Nine Eaves usually did.

The first leaned low over a broom and cut around the western chimney in a polished brown arc. The second sat upright on another, rising at a measured angle while the lacquered handle stayed level beneath both hands. The third went past between the lifted wings of a pale horse, hands buried in its mane while each downstroke sent a warm gust rolling over the slates.

Two brooms were not a coincidence. Nine Eaves kept racks of practice models, broom-width gates, and enough standard diagrams to wallpaper a tower. The horse was rare enough to draw looks in the dining hall, but not questions on an assessment roof. Its lane was painted wider, its harness had already passed inspection, and everyone present knew what those wings could do.

Then there was me.

“Juni Wex,” Dovek called again.

“Present. Still regrettably attached to the building.”

The Collegium of Nine Eaves occupied most of the view below us: black roofs pitched at improbable angles, bridges stitching tower to tower, windows bright as chips of amber. Beyond it, the city fell away in terraces toward a silver bend of river. The launch roof was so high that birds passed beneath the gutters. Prestige, I had learned, was often ordinary terror with excellent masonry.

I sat on the warm slate and unlaced my shoes. Mine were scuffed brown leather, bought without enchantment, one still bearing a pale water mark from a badly judged fountain.

I pulled them off, set my stockinged feet on the roof, and turned the right shoe heel-up across my knee.

Dovek crouched opposite me. Their examination coat snapped once in the wind and settled. “Begin.”

The ink stylus came from my cuff. I pressed its blunt nib beside the heel and drew the first stroke in a curve around the back of the shoe. The second hooked across the underside toward the arch. The third doubled inward, a black curl aimed at the small hollow between them. It looked less like a word than an arrow teaching the wind where to leave.

Nothing happened. Ink was only ink until someone living asked more of it.

I cupped the shoe between both hands, breathed, and let warmth run out through my palms. The three lines drank it. For an instant, black deepened beyond black.

I drew the mirrored wind curl around the other heel and underside, charged it, and put both shoes back on. My fingers trembled at the laces. Apparently fear was mostly an audience with opinions.

Dovek tapped one gloved finger above the right-hand curl. “No crown.”

“I’m fond of steering.”

“And your stationary count?”

“Small bursts.”

I traced the shape I had omitted: a shallow cap with three points. “A crown spreads one heel’s wind beneath my center. It will check a fall and quiet a turn, but it cannot steer. Once I feed it power, one point burns away per breath. Three points, exactly three breaths, then the crown is gone and the narrow jet returns.”

“Can you interrupt it?”

“I can cut power, but the unused points burn out anyway. It cannot be restarted.”

“A limitation.”

“A feature with strict opinions about counting.”

“A limitation,” Dovek repeated. “You are required to remain inside the stationary boundary for a count of three. Demonstrate the limitation. Do not conceal it.”

The first broom candidate flashed past the far eave, coat streaming straight behind. Above, the second held almost motionless while the broom’s bristles trembled through corrections too small to see. The pale horse climbed through a patch of sun, every feather briefly edged in gold.

I imagined a wide, blunt plume roaring beneath me while I hung unable to turn, all three crown points visibly burning away. Effective, temporary, and about as elegant as being held aloft by an argument.

“Understood,” I said.

I did understand. I simply had no intention of doing it.

* * *

Dovek raised a hand.

I ran for the edge.

At the gutter, I jumped, pointed both soles down, and drove warmth through my legs.

The curls answered.

Two pale streams of wind tore from my heels. They snapped my coat against my back, flung grit from the gutter, and punched me upward so hard my stomach arrived a moment after the rest of me.

I made a sound that began as a scream and improved into laughter.

The shoes did not carry me. The ink did not decide where I went. I supplied the power; the curls narrowed it into two rushing jets; my feet aimed the result. With both soles turned toward the roof and the output matched, I climbed. When I swept my heels behind me, the streams bent backward and shoved me forward into the blue.

For three glorious seconds, everything worked.

Then I drove a shade too much power through my left leg. Its jet surged harder.

My left hip lifted. My right shoulder dropped. The western chimney tipped sideways in front of me as I rolled toward the weaker stream.

“Excellent,” I told the rapidly rotating school. “A view.”

I nearly answered by forcing more through both heels. Instead I eased my left leg and fed the right until the two pale currents matched. The roll slowed. I opened my arms, shifted my hips, and came level with enough dignity to fool anyone who had not seen the first half.

The course turned around a tall iron arch strung with blue streamers. The first broom candidate banked through it by leaning into the curved handle. The second rose in a straight, measured line, hands quiet on the grip. Higher still, the winged horse folded its wings for one clean heartbeat, then opened them and surged upward.

There are respectable ways to fly. I had watched them practiced from the lower courts for years: the long broom bank, the patient broom hover, the powerful bargain between a rider and a winged animal. They all looked as though the sky were a country one might enter with the correct papers.

I arrived with two handwritten winds shouting at my heels.
